questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the female body is considered the most reliable indicator among the given options?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch, also known as the Pouch of Douglas, is the most dependent (reliant) part of the female peritoneal cavity in the upright position. It is located between the posterior wall of the uterus and the anterior wall of the rectum. Because it is the lowest point, clinical conditions such as hemoperitoneum, pelvic inflammatory disease exudates, or ruptured ectopic pregnancies result in fluid accumulation here. The posterior fornix (Option C) is the deepest part of the vagina and is anatomically related to this pouch, making it the site for culdocentesis. The ovarian fossa (Option B) is a depression in the lateral pelvic wall where the ovary sits but is not a dependent drainage area. The vesicouterine pouch (Option D) is located anteriorly between the bladder and uterus and is shallower and higher than the Pouch of Douglas. Therefore, in clinical diagnostics and imaging, the rectouterine pouch is the primary site checked for pathological fluid collection
questions.learning: The rectouterine pouch, also known as the Pouch of Douglas, is the most dependent (reliant) part of the female peritoneal cavity in the upright position.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The most likely cause is accidental endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus, resulting in ventilation of only the right lung and subsequent collapse (atelectasis) of the left lung.
options: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
Pneumothorax on the left side due to positive pressure ventilation
questions.explanation: The absence of breath sounds on the left side with sounds heard only on the right immediately following intubation strongly supports a diagnosis of right endobronchial (mainstem) intubation. This occurs because the right mainstem bronchus is more vertically oriented than the left, making it the most likely path if an endotracheal tube is advanced too far. This results in selective ventilation of the right lung only, while the left lung collapses due to lack of air entry. Mucus secretions (Option B) would typically cause bilateral decreased air entry or generalized poor air movement rather than such distinct unilateral findings. Left-sided pneumothorax (Option C) could cause unilateral sound loss but would usually feature additional signs like hyperresonance and tracheal deviation. Bronchospasm (Option D) presents with bilateral wheezing and increased airway pressures rather than complete unilateral absence of breath sounds. Withdrawing the tube slightly usually resolves the issue
questions.learning: The absence of breath sounds on the left side with sounds heard only on the right immediately following intubation strongly supports a diagnosis of right endobronchial (mainstem) intubation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the schedule of the OPV vaccine?
questions.explanation: As per the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) in India, the primary series of the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) consists of three doses administered at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age. These are typically given alongside other primary vaccines like Pentavalent and Rotavirus. A booster dose of OPV is later given at 16–24 months. Regarding the distractors, the 9th month (Options B and C) is the timing for the first dose of the Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine and the newly introduced third dose of fIPV (fractional Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine), but not for a standard primary OPV dose. Option D is a vague range that does not align with the standardized multi-dose schedule. Therefore, the specific 6-10-14 week interval is the universally accepted primary schedule for OPV in public health programs
questions.learning: As per the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) in India, the primary series of the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) consists of three doses administered at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the management of an unruptured ectopic pregnancy, which scenario is not appropriate for expectant management?
options: Initial serum beta hCG level < 1000 mIU/ mL
questions.explanation: Expectant management (observation) for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is only appropriate for a highly select, stable group of patients where spontaneous resolution is likely. Standard criteria for this approach include the patient being asymptomatic (Option C), having low and decreasing serum beta-hCG levels (Option D), and an initial hCG level ideally below 1000 mIU/mL (Option A). A gestational sac size greater than 4 cm (Option B) is a definitive contraindication for expectant management and even for medical management (methotrexate). Large sac sizes carry a significantly higher risk of rupture and internal hemorrhage, necessitating surgical intervention (salpingectomy or salpingostomy). Options A, C, and D are all favorable indicators for a trial of observation. Therefore, because a large sac indicates an advanced ectopic pregnancy that is unstable, Option B is the correct "does not indicate" choice
questions.learning: Expectant management (observation) for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is only appropriate for a highly select, stable group of patients where spontaneous resolution is likely.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient develops a recurrent skin rash at the same site after taking NSAIDs for knee pain and reports a similar episode at the identical location six months earlier following NSAID use for back pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The description of a skin lesion that recurs at the exact same anatomical site whenever the specific causative drug is taken is the hallmark of a fixed drug eruption (FDE) (Option C). FDEs typically appear as well-circumscribed, round or oval, erythematous or dusky-red patches that may occasionally blister. Common triggers include NSAIDs (like the case described), sulfonamides, and tetracyclines. After the initial lesion heals, it often leaves a patch of gray or brown post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (Option B), which is a consequence rather than the primary diagnosis. General drug hypersensitivity (Option A) would more likely present as a widespread rash (e.g., urticaria or exanthematous eruption). Drug-induced hypermelanosis (Option D) involves generalized skin darkening rather than recurrent localized patches. The site-specific recurrence is pathognomonic for FDE, believed to be due to localized memory T-cells remaining in the skin
questions.learning: The description of a skin lesion that recurs at the exact same anatomical site whenever the specific causative drug is taken is the hallmark of a fixed drug eruption (FDE) (Option C).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presented with bilateral proptosis, restriction of eye movements, and chemosis. Her thyroid profile showed she was euthyroid. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroid ophthalmopathy

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of thyroid ophthalmopathy.

Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult in the euthyroid state. The main features of TED include lid retraction, proptosis, periorbital edema, chemosis, and restrictive myopathy.

Other options-

Option A- Orbital pseudotumor presents with painful eye movements periorbital edema, erythema, proptosis, ptosis, diplopia.

Option C- Orbital lymphoma usually presents in the 7th decade, most commonly observed as a painless palpable mass in the superolateral quadrant.

Option D- Orbital cellulitis is usually a unilateral condition with pain, proptosis, and chemosis.

NOTE: Thyroid eye disease can also, though less commonly, occur in euthyroid patients.
questions.learning: Thyroid ophthalmopathy — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of thyroid ophthalmopathy. Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult in the euthyroid state.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old female came with complaints of primary amenorrhoea. She had normal secondary sexual characteristics and breast development corresponded to Tanner stage IV. Her FSH - 5.3 and LH - 12.1. Her karyotype is 46XX. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mullerian agenesis

The given clinical scenario is that of a female with primary amenorrhea, preservation of secondary characteristics, and normal levels of FSH and LH, with a karyotype of 46XX. These are features of Mullerian agenesis.

Congenital absence of both the uterus and vagina is termed Mullerian agenesis or Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. Females have a shallow vaginal pouch (1 to 2 inches deep). The uterus, cervix, and upper part of the vagina are absent. Typically, normal ovaries persist, as they originate from the genital ridge. Individual presents with primary amenorrhea, have a normal female appearance, secondary sexual characteristics, and 46 XX karyotype. Most patients with Mullerian agenesis have only small rudimentary Mullerian bulbs without endometrial activity.

With Mullerian agenesis, traditional conception is not possible, but pregnancy may be achieved using oocyte retrieval, fertilization, and gestational surrogacy.

Individuals with Mullerian agenesis or hypoplasia have associated congenital renal or skeletal anomalies. Common renal anomalies include ectopic, horseshoe or pelvic kidney and collecting system anomalies. Skeletal malformations include spina bifida, sacralization, sacral bone lumbarization, and cervical vertebral anomalies.

Other options:

Option A - Kallmann syndrome presents with primary amenorrhea due to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from deficiency of GnRH. The FSH and LH levels are lower than normal, leading to poor development of secondary sexual characteristics. It is associated with olfactory dysfunction and anosmia.

Option B - Androgen insensitivity syndrome occurs due to a defect in the androgen receptor in a genotypic male (XY). These individuals are phenotypic females with no male or female internal genitalia. They have normal female external genitalia with an absent or shallow vagina, well-developed breasts, and scanty body hair (axillary and pubic) and present with primary amenorrhea.

Option C - Gonadal dysgenesis in the form of 45XO (Turner syndrome) or 46XY (Swyer syndrome) presents with poor development of secondary sexual characteristics. Since the gonads are nonfunctional, there is a loss of negative feedback with increased levels of FSH and LH.
questions.learning: Mullerian agenesis — The given clinical scenario is that of a female with primary amenorrhea, preservation of secondary characteristics, and normal levels of FSH and LH, with a karyotype of 46XX.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the use of the instrument given below:
options: For ligation of uterine artery during hysterectomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. For tubal ligation

The given instrument is a fallope ring applicator. It is used in tubal ligation.

Falope ring sterilization is accomplished by applying silicone rubber bands to the fallopian tubes. The major advantage is the elimination of thermocoagulation. The occlusion is only in a short segment and can allow for tubal reconstruction.
questions.learning: For tubal ligation — The given instrument is a fallope ring applicator. Falope ring sterilization is accomplished by applying silicone rubber bands to the fallopian tubes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Match the following disorders causing secondary amenorrhoea with their respective lab findings.

Condition
Lab markers

1. Sheehan's syndrome
A. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol

2. Premature Ovarian failure
B. High LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

3. PCOS
C. Low LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

4. Asherman's syndrome
D. High LH, High FSH, Low estradiol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A

The correct answer is 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A.

Condition
Lab markers

1. Sheehan's syndrome
C. Low LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

2. Premature Ovarian failure
D. High LH, High FSH, Low estradiol

3. PCOS
B. High LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

4. Asherman's syndrome
A. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol

Secondary amenorrhoea is the absence of menses for more than three months in girls or women who previously had regular menstrual cycles or six months in girls or women who had irregular menses.

Premature Ovarian failure or premature menopause is the development of menopause before the age of 40 years. It is diagnosed when at least 2 serum FSH levels are elevated (>40 mIU/l) when measured at least 1 month apart in a woman <40 years. The other findings consistent with POF include low estradiol and an elevated FSH/LH ratio.

Asherman's syndrome is the presence of uterine synechiae, due to the destruction of large areas of the endometrium, most commonly as a result of trauma to the endometrium following pregnancy-related curettages. Oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, abortion, and infertility are seen with uterine synechiae. The laboratory investigations and hormonal assays are generally normal in isolated cases of uterine synechiae. Diagnosis is generally established using hysteroscopy. Moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography suggests a diagnosis of Asherman syndrome. Treatment is by hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

PCOS is a multisystem, metabolic, endocrine dysfunction that commonly occurs among women in the reproductive age group. The endocrinological changes reflecting in the assays are summarized in the pearl attached below.

Sheehan's syndrome/ pituitary apoplexy is hemorrhagic infarction of large pituitary adenomas or pituitary infarction due to traumatic major blood loss. If this blood loss occurs during delivery, it's called Sheehan's syndrome. Affected women may present with panhypopituitarism and may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent among symptoms are lactation failure (due to deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to deficiency of gonadotropins).

Note: Estradiol level in PCOS is low in comparison to Estrone (E1).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient sustained blunt trauma to the eye 6 months ago and now presents with double vision. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iriododialysis

The given image shows iridodialysis.

Iridodialysis refers to detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil. A black biconvex area is seen at the periphery at the site of detachment.

The given image depicts iridodialysis and a D-shaped pupil.

Other Options:

Option A: Cycloiriditis is inflammation involving both the ciliary body and iris, leading to pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. It's characterized by cells and flare in the anterior chamber, keratic precipitates, and possible synechiae formation.

Option B: Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens. It is usually seen after blunt trauma to the eye and orbit.

Option D: Coloboma is a congenital anomaly, that develops due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It is characterized by poorly developed uveal tissue. These colobomas may involve the optic nerve, choroid, retina, and iris.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: For how long is exclusive breastfeeding recommended?
questions.explanation: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (India), exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months of an infant's life. "Exclusive" means that the infant receives only breast milk; no other liquids or solids are given, not even water, with the exception of oral rehydration solutions, drops, or syrups of vitamins, minerals, or medicines. Breast milk provides all the nutrients, antibodies, and fluids a healthy infant needs during this critical growth period. Option A (3 months) is insufficient for optimal development and immune protection. Options C and D (9 and 12 months) are incorrect as a primary goal; while breastfeeding should continue alongside complementary foods up to 2 years or beyond, "exclusive" breastfeeding must end at 6 months to introduce essential nutrients like iron that breast milk alone can no longer adequately provide. This practice significantly reduces infant mortality from common childhood illnesses like diarrhea and pneumonia
questions.learning: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (India), exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months of an infant's life.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding Budd-Chiari Syndrome (BCS)?
options: Venous drainage of the liver is occluded by IVC thrombus.
Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features.

Budd–Chiari syndrome (BCS) is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with the right atrium. The obstruction leads to hepatic congestion, portal hypertension, and impaired liver function.

The classic clinical triad consists of:

• Abdominal pain/discomfort
• Ascites
• Hepatomegaly

Why not the other options?

• A. It principally affects young males: BCS is more common in young to middle-aged adults, with a female predominance in many populations due to associations with pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, and myeloproliferative disorders.
• B. Venous drainage of the liver is occluded by IVC thrombus: The obstruction most commonly involves the hepatic veins. IVC obstruction can occur but is not the defining or usual mechanism.
• C. Quadrate lobe (Segment 4 and 5) undergoes hypertrophy: The caudate lobe (Segment I) undergoes hypertrophy because it has independent venous drainage directly into the IVC, allowing it to remain relatively spared.
questions.learning: Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features. Budd–Chiari syndrome (BCS) is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with the right atrium.

questions.text: Which part of this bone is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa?

The part of the scapula marked as 1 is the coracoid process and it is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa. The tip of the coracoid process lies approximately 2.5 cm below the clavicle, immediately lateral to the infraclavicular fossa (deltopectoral triangle). Hence, the coracoid process can be palpated below the clavicle.

The coracoid process arises from the upper border of the neck of the scapula and it projects forwards and slightly laterally. Attachments at the coracoid process include

• The conoid portion of the coracoclavicular ligament
• Pectoralis minor
• Medial end of coraco-acromial ligament
• Coracohumeral ligament
• Glenocorocoid ligament

Other options

Option B - Acromian process continues from the spine of the scapula. The acromion is subcutaneous over its dorsal surface, The attachments at the acromion are the coracoacromial ligament, the articular capsule of the acromioclavicular joint, and horizontal fibers of the trapezius.

Option C - The glenoid fossa is present at the lateral angle of the scapula. It is articular with the humerus to form the shoulder joint.

Option D - The inferior angle lies over the seventh rib. Dorsally, it is related to latissimus dorsi. The angle is visible when the arm is raised over the head.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 2-year-old boy was brought to the emergency when his mother noticed that he had developed dusky appearance and lethargy over the past 6–8 hours. The child had been prescribed some medicine for vomiting by a local practitioner. Examination revealed normal sized pupils reacting to light, GCS 9, and shallow breathing with cyanosis. Arterial blood gas revealed a PaO₂ of 80 mmHg and SpO₂ of 60%. Which one of the following drugs may be implicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metoclopramide

The child has cyanosis with a markedly low SpO₂ (60%) despite a relatively preserved PaO₂ (80 mmHg), suggesting methemoglobinemia.

Metoclopramide can rarely cause methemoglobinemia, particularly in young children, due to oxidation of hemoglobin from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, impairing oxygen delivery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Domperidone: Not classically associated with methemoglobinemia. Its important adverse effects include QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias.
• B. Granisetron: A 5-HT₃ antagonist used as an antiemetic. It is mainly associated with headache, constipation, and QT prolongation, not methemoglobinemia.
• C. Aprepitant: An NK₁ receptor antagonist. It can cause fatigue, hiccups, and drug interactions, but methemoglobinemia is not a characteristic toxicity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man, working in a dye manufacturing industry, presents with urinary complaints. Ultrasound shows markedly thickened and irregular bladder walls. What is the most definitive management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient's occupational history as a dye manufacturing worker is a classic risk factor for developing bladder cancer (exposure to aromatic amines). The ultrasound finding of thickened and irregular bladder walls in a symptomatic older male strongly suggests muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). For MIBC, the most definitive management approach is Radical cystectomy (removal of the bladder and associated lymph nodes) with urinary diversion. Cystoscopy with transurethral removal (TURBT) (Option A) is used for initial diagnosis and treatment of non-muscle-invasive disease. BCG instillation (Option B) and intravesical Mitomycin C (Option D) are adjuvant therapies for non-muscle-invasive tumors to prevent recurrence. Because MIBC has a high risk of systemic spread, radical surgery is necessary for a potential cure. This often follows neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy to improve survival. Recognizing high-risk occupational histories is vital for suspecting aggressive bladder malignancies in the clinical setting
questions.learning: The patient's occupational history as a dye manufacturing worker is a classic risk factor for developing bladder cancer (exposure to aromatic amines).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with a history of poor dental hygiene undergoes tooth extraction and develops low-grade fever with a new-onset heart murmur two weeks later. Blood cultures show alpha-hemolytic gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. Which organism is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Streptococcus viridans

Streptococcus viridans is a group of gram-positive cocci arranged in chains, often a common cause of infective endocarditis, particularly in cases of subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Streptococcus viridans is a part of the normal flora of the human mouth, throat, and upper respiratory tract. They are alpha-hemolytic, meaning they cause partial hemolysis on blood agar, resulting in a greenish colouration of the agar, hence the name "viridans," which means "green" in Latin.

Although Viridans streptococci are typically susceptible to penicillin, certain strains may exhibit resistance. Therefore, it is crucial that when dealing with endocarditis, the specific strain responsible is identified, and its sensitivity to antibiotics is assessed. This ensures the selection of suitable antibiotics at effective bactericidal levels for treatment.

Other options:

Option A) Staphylococcus aureus is  Beta-hemolytic, and appears in grape-like clusters, not chains. It causes acute endocarditiswith rapid valve destruction, usually in IV drug users.

Option B) Streptococcus pyogenes is also beta-hemolytic, not alpha. It is the Group A Streptococcus causing pharyngitis, impetigo, and rheumatic fever.

Option C) Streptococcus pneumoniae is Alpha-hemolytic but appears as lancet-shaped diplococci, not chains. It is optochin sensitive and causes pneumonia, meningitis, and otitis media.

Pearl PF1994: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Pathologic criteria

* Clinical criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when:

* Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR

* If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which medication should be preferred for a 45-year-old chronic alcoholic with a history of liver cirrhosis, admitted with fever and abdominal pain, and found to have ascitic fluid neutrophil count of 360 cells/µL?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP), a common and serious complication of cirrhosis. SBP is diagnosed when the ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is . In this patient, the count is 360, confirming the diagnosis. Cefotaxime, a third-generation cephalosporin, is the first-line antibiotic of choice for SBP. It provides excellent coverage against common gram-negative aerobic organisms like E. coli and Klebsiella, which are the most frequent causes. Metronidazole (Option B) targets anaerobes, which are rarely involved in SBP. Amoxicillin (Option C) has poor penetration and high resistance rates in this setting. Vancomycin (Option D) is reserved for suspected MRSA or failed initial therapy. Because Cefotaxime is highly effective, has low toxicity, and is proven to improve survival in cirrhotic patients with peritonitis, it is the definitive treatment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a fracture visible on X-ray. In this type of fracture, which nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a spiral fracture of the humerus midshaft. This fracture type is notoriously associated with injury to the radial nerve because the nerve courses directly against the bone within the spiral (radial) groove. Trauma at this specific location frequently causes radial nerve palsy, which manifests clinically as "wrist drop"—the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. The median nerve (Option A) is situated medially and is rarely affected by midshaft humeral injuries. The ulnar nerve (Option C) runs near the medial epicondyle and is more commonly injured in distal fractures. The axillary nerve (Option D) is located near the surgical neck of the humerus and is typically injured in proximal fractures or shoulder dislocations. Given the close anatomical proximity of the radial nerve to the humeral shaft, it is the most likely structure to be damaged
questions.learning: The X-ray displays a spiral fracture of the humerus midshaft. This fracture type is notoriously associated with injury to the radial nerve because the nerve courses directly against the bone within the spiral (radial) groove.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person comes to the OPD with a burn injury to the right thigh. On examination, a soddened injury is seen along with erythema, blisters, and a line of demarcation that extends down the limb. What is the most likely cause of the injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Moist heat

The soddened injury with erythema, blisters, and a line of demarcation that extends down the limb is highly suggestive of a scald injury caused by moist heat.

Scald injury is an injury that results from the application of liquid above 60°C or from steam i.e moist heat. Redness appears immediately followed by blistering in a few minutes. Removal of the blistered skin leaves a raw, pink surface. Blisters are surrounded by a hyperaemic zone. Scalds appear soddened and bleached but the hair does not get singed. The skin does not get blackened or charred.

Scald injuries are limited to the area of contact and are more severe at the initial point of contact. It can occur through clothing, which worsens damage due to a longer period of contact with the hot liquid and a reduced cooling effect of evaporation.

It can be

• Immersion burns: Accidental or deliberate immersion in hot liquid, usually water.
• Splash or spill burns: Usually accidental.
• Steam burns: Exposure to superheated steam.

Clinical degree of scalding:

• Erythema (reddening)
• Vesication (blister formation)
• Necrosis of dermis when deeper layers of skin are involved.

The image below shows a scald burn due to moist heat.

Other options:

Option A: Electric burns are injuries caused due to electric current, characterized by puckering of the skin at the edges of the burns. It is surrounded by an area of pallor. There is no red line at the point of entry and exit. The characteristic marks seen at the entry point are called Joule burns, or electrical burns/marks. They are chalky white, shallow, centrally collapsed blisters with a raised border.

The image below shows electric marks.

Option B: Chemical burns by acid or alkalis appear as ulcerated patches without blisters. The hair is not singed and the red line of demarcation is absent. Sometimes, the burn shows distinct coloration and is usually uniform in character. Strong acids produce dark leathery burns on the skin. Strong alkalis cause the skin to slough and leave moist, slimy, greyish areas.

Option C: Dry heat injuries are caused by a flame, via direct conduction or radiation to the skin. These are characterized by singeing of the hair and blackening of the skin. Vesication may or may not be present.
questions.learning: Moist heat — The soddened injury with erythema, blisters, and a line of demarcation that extends down the limb is highly suggestive of a scald injury caused by moist heat.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The "Carpet Tack Sign" is observed in which of the following conditions? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE)

Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) is a chronic cutaneous form of lupus characterized by well-defined erythematous plaques with adherent scales, follicular plugging, atrophy, and scarring.

Carpet Tack Sign

• Seen when the adherent scale is lifted from a DLE lesion.
• The undersurface of the scale shows multiple horny plugs corresponding to dilated hair follicles.
• This appearance resembles the underside of a carpet tack, hence the name Carpet Tack Sign (also called the Tin Tack Sign).

Clinical Features of DLE

• Erythematous scaly plaques
• Follicular plugging
• Central atrophy and scarring
• Dyspigmentation
• Commonly affects face, scalp, and ears

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

Pityriasis Versicolor

• Caused by Malassezia species.
• Shows fine branny scales and positive scratch sign.

Psoriasis: Characterized by silvery-white scales and Auspitz sign.

Lichen Planus: Characterized by violaceous papules with Wickham striae.
questions.learning: Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) is a chronic cutaneous form of lupus characterized by well-defined erythematous plaques with adherent scales, follicular plugging, atrophy, and scarring.

Correct answer: A. Functional residual capacity

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person was stabbed in the anterior thigh and later died. The body is brought for postmortem examination. What type of injury is this classified as?
questions.explanation: A penetrating wound occurs when a sharp object, such as a knife, pierces the skin and enters deeper tissues or a body cavity. In this case, the stab to the anterior thigh involves depth that is greater than the surface length of the wound, which characterizes it as a stab or penetrating injury. Regarding the distractors, an incised wound (Option A) is a clean cut that is typically longer on the skin surface than it is deep. A puncture wound (Option (C) is generally used to describe stabs involving only soft tissues without entering a body cavity or viscus, though "penetrating" is a more comprehensive medical term for this fatal injury. Blunt force injury (Option D) involves trauma from non-sharp objects like clubs or hammers and does not involve the sharp penetration seen in stabbing. Since the injury was deep enough to cause death, it is classified as a penetrating stab wound

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: X-ray of a patient appears as below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lung collapse

In the provided X-ray image, there is evidence of complete opacification (whitening) of the left lung field, along with a shift of the mediastinum (central structure in the chest containing the heart and major blood vessels) towards the affected side. These findings are indicative of a lung collapse, also known as atelectasis.

Other Options:

Option A: Pneumonia may present with airspace opacification in the lungs, but it usually does not result in complete opacification of an entire lung field as seen in the provided image.

Option B: Pleural effusion typically appears as a blunting of the costophrenic angles or as increased opacity at the lung bases on a chest X-ray.

Option D: Hydropneumothorax refers to the presence of both fluid (hydrop) and air (pneumo) in the pleural space. While it can cause lung collapse, it typically presents with a combination of radiographic findings indicating both air and fluid in the pleural space, such as an air-fluid level or a meniscus sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An MRCP image is shown below. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Choledocholithiasis

The given MRCP image shows multiple round filling defects within the common bile duct indicative of choledocholithiasis.

Choledocholithiasis or common bile duct stones are classified based on their point of origin. Choledocholithiasis is mostly clinically silent but may present with biliary colic and even obstructive jaundice. Management of choledocholithiasis includes ERCP +/- sphincterotomy followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

MRCP uses the fluid which is present in the biliary and pancreatic ducts as a contrast agent and does not require external contrast material administered into the ductal system. It is a non-invasive investigation for evaluating extrahepatic, intrahepatic bile duct, and pancreatic duct. No interventions are performed under MRCP.

MRCP uses T2 weighted  MRI and it recognizes slow-flowing or stationary fluid within ducts, which appear brighter relative to adjacent solid tissues. MRCP can be used to evaluate various conditions of the pancreaticobiliary ductal system, examples include:

• Congenital anomalies of the cystic and hepatic ducts
• Post-surgical biliary anatomy
• Pancreas divisum
• Anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction
• Choledocholithiasis
• Biliary structures
• Chronic pancreatitis
• Pancreatic cystic lesions
• Trauma to the biliary system

MRCP in benign strictures would typically show smooth elongated tapering of the bile duct, while malignancy-associated strictures typically show abrupt shouldering.
questions.learning: Choledocholithiasis — The given MRCP image shows multiple round filling defects within the common bile duct indicative of choledocholithiasis. Choledocholithiasis or common bile duct stones are classified based on their point of origin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bainbridge reflex

Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is Bainbridge Reflex.

The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain. Then efferent signals are transmitted back through vagal and sympathetic nerves to increase heart rate and strength of heart contraction. Thus, this reflex helps prevent damming of blood in the veins, atria, and pulmonary circulation.

Other options:

Option A: Bezold–Jarisch Reflex: Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers in the cardiopulmonary region causes profound bradycardia, hypotension and a brief period of apnoea followed by rapid shallow breathing.

Option C: Cushing Reflex: When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to Rostral Ventro-Lateral Medulla (RVLM) neurons is compromised. The local hypoxia and hypercapnia cause an increase in discharge from the neurons, producing hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.

Option D: J Reflex: The stimulation of the J-receptors (C receptors/juxta-pulmonary capillary receptors) causes apnea followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia, and hypotension.
questions.learning: Bainbridge reflex Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is Bainbridge Reflex. The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a heme breakdown product?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ALA

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; rather it is an intermediate in the synthesis of heme molecules.

The process of heme breakdown occurs over a series of reactions. In the reticuloendothelial system of the liver, spleen and bone marrow, heme is degraded by microsomal heme oxygenase. It requires NADPH and cytochrome c. In this process, the alpha methenyl bridge of the heme molecule is liberated as carbon monoxide. The Fe+ liberated is oxidized to Fe3+++ and taken up by transferrin.

The linear tetrapyrrole formed is biliverdin (green pigment), which is further reduced to bilirubin (red-yellow pigment) by an NADPH-dependent biliverdin reductase. The bilirubin is transported in the plasma bound to albumin and is taken up by the liver, where it is conjugated with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble, which is finally excreted in the bile.

The intestinal bacteria deconjugate the bilirubin, which is reduced to urobilinogen. It is further reduced to stercobilinogen, which is excreted through feces.
questions.learning: ALA Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; rather it is an intermediate in the synthesis of heme molecules. The process of heme breakdown occurs over a series of reactions.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency room after an RTA with a history of diplopia, epistaxis, and restricted eye movements. The radiological examination is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Orbital floor fracture

The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Blowout fractures are isolated comminuted fractures caused by direct trauma to the orbit that result in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure. This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall, which is usually the posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fractures is the medial wall of the orbit.

An isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called a blowout fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum into the maxillary sinus, which may lead to enophthalmos and entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle. The floor is made of zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones.

The patient with a blowout fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paraesthesia along the infraorbital nerve is also very common. Clinical signs: periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis, and subconjunctival haemorrhage. Infraorbital hypoesthesia may be present because of entrapment of the infraorbital nerve.

Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called the "hanging drop sign" or "teardrop sign".

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics.

Le Fort fracture is the term used to describe different types of maxillary fractures.

Investigations:

* X-ray (Water's view) shows a teardrop opacity in the maxillary sinus.

* A CT scan is used to confirm the site and size of the fracture and entrapment of muscle.

* Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants.

Indications of surgery:

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

* Persistent and progressive diplopia in the primary position

* Entrapment of orbital contents

* Large fracture involving at least half of the orbital floor

If any of these conditions are present, surgical correction is required within 2 weeks.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the parasite from the given life cycle.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fasciola hepatica

The given life cycle belongs to Fasciola hepatica.

Fasciola hepatica (sheep liver fluke) causes disease primarily in sheep and other domestic animals. Humans are infected by eating watercress (or other aquatic plants) contaminated by larvae (metacercariae) that excyst in the duodenum, penetrate the gut wall, and reach the liver, where they mature into adults.

The adult flukes in the bile ducts produce eggs, which are excreted in the feces. The eggs hatch in freshwater and miracidia enter the snails. Miracidia develop into cercariae, which then encyst on aquatic vegetation. Sheep and humans eat the plants, thus completing the life cycle. Most infections are asymptomatic. Halzoun is a painful pharyngitis caused by the presence of adult flukes on the posterior pharyngeal wall after eating raw sheep liver. Obstructive jaundice can occur months or years later.

Diagnosis is made by identification of the eggs in the feces.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old primigravida at 41+3 weeks of gestation is brought to the emergency department by her family after prolonged labor at home. She has been in labor for 18 hours with strong contractions. On examination, she is dehydrated, with a pulse of 126/min, blood pressure of 90/58 mmHg, and temperature of 100°F. The uterus is tense and contracted, and a tight ring is palpable per abdomen. Fetal parts are not felt, and the fetal heart rate is 100 bpm with late decelerations. What is this ring?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bandl's ring

The patient has prolonged labor, dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, a tense contracted uterus, fetal distress with late decelerations, and a palpable pathological ring, all of which are features of obstructed labor. The ring felt per abdomen is Bandl’s ring, which is typically seen in obstructed labor.

Bandl's ring/ Pathological retraction ring:

* In obstructed labour, the upper segment of the uterus contracts and retracts vigorously in an attempt to overcome the obstruction while the lower segment dilates.

* With each contraction, there is myometrial shortening so that the actively contracting upper segment becomes progressively thicker and shorter. The passive lower segment is progressively stretched and becomes thinner.

* The junction between the two segments stands out prominently as a pathological retraction ring/Bandl ring.

Other options:

Option A and C: Constriction ring/Schroeder's ring/ contraction ring is formed due to incoordinate uterine contraction (abnormal polarity) when there is localized spastic contraction of a ring of circular muscle fibers of the uterus. It is formed due to injudicious use of oxytocin and premature rupture of membranes (PROM). The upper segment contracts and retracts with relaxation and the lower segment remains thick and loose.

Option D: After each contraction of the upper segment, the muscles do not return to their previous length, but tension remains essentially the same. By comparison, in the lower segment, successive lengthening of the fibers with labor is accompanied by thinning, normally to only a few millimeters in the thinnest part. As a result of the lower segment thinning and concomitant upper segment thickening, a boundary between the two is marked by a ridge on the inner uterine surface - the physiological retraction ring.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is being treated with indomethacin and is also on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. Which adverse effect is most likely to occur due to this drug combination?
questions.explanation: The concurrent use of an ACE inhibitor (like enalapril) and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) like indomethacin significantly increases the risk of hyperkalemia. ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion by blocking angiotensin II production, which leads to decreased potassium excretion. Indomethacin further worsens this by inhibiting renal prostaglandins, which normally maintain renal blood flow and support potassium secretion. The combination effectively impairs the body's ability to clear potassium, potentially leading to cardiac arrhythmias. Hypercalcemia (Option B) is not a standard side effect of either drug. Hypernatremia (Option C) is unlikely because ACE inhibitors promote mild sodium excretion (natriuresis). Hyperphosphatemia (Option D) is typically a complication of chronic kidney disease rather than a direct drug-drug interaction between these classes. Therefore, serum potassium levels must be closely monitored in patients on this combination therapy
questions.learning: The concurrent use of an ACE inhibitor (like enalapril) and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) like indomethacin significantly increases the risk of hyperkalemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman with a past history of rheumatic fever is found on examination to have a loud first heart sound and a mid-diastolic murmur. Which valvular heart disease is most likely present?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of rheumatic fever combined with the auscultatory findings of a loud S1 and a mid-diastolic murmur are classic indicators of Mitral Stenosis (MS). Rheumatic heart disease is the leading cause of MS worldwide, resulting in the thickening and fusion of valve leaflets. The S1 is loud because the stiffened valves close forcefully at the start of systole. The mid-diastolic murmur occurs due to turbulent blood flow across the narrowed mitral orifice as the left ventricle fills. While Tricuspid Stenosis (TS) (Option A) also produces a mid-diastolic murmur, it typically increases with inspiration and is rarely seen in isolation. Mitral Regurgitation (MR) (Option B) presents with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Aortic Regurgitation (AR) (Option D) produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Therefore, based on the specific location and nature of the murmur following rheumatic fever, Mitral Stenosis is the most accurate diagnosis for this patient
questions.learning: The patient’s history of rheumatic fever combined with the auscultatory findings of a loud S1 and a mid-diastolic murmur are classic indicators of Mitral Stenosis (MS).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate was brought with yellow sclera and hypoglycemia. He is exclusively breastfed. Urine Benedict's test is positive. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this neonate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase

Features of jaundice and hypoglycemia in a neonate who is breastfed, suggest a diagnosis of Classic Galactosemia, in which there is a deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.

Classic galactosemia:

* Deficiency of galactose-1-uridyltransferase leads to the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol

* Infants show vomiting, diarrhea, and poor weight gain within 3-4 days of breastfeeding

* Jaundice and liver dysfunction appear in the first or second week of life.

* Proximal renal tubular disease may also manifest as metabolic acidosis, galactosuria, glucosuria, and aminoaciduria

* Most common cause of death is E.coli sepsis

* Acute galactose toxicity is manifested by neurological symptoms

* Diagnosis is made by genetic or mutational analysis. There will be presence of reducing substances in the urine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 75-year-old man with prostate carcinoma presents to you with a PSA of 9 ng/mL with a small tumor focus. His Gleason score is 6. What will be your most likely management?

PSA- Prostate-specific antigen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Active surveillance

The given clinical vignette of a 75-year-old man, with a low PSA (<10 ng/ml), Gleason score of 6, and a small tumor focus point to a diagnosis of low-risk prostatic carcinoma. The most likely management for this patient would be active surveillance only.

Active surveillance is done when there is:

• Gleason score of 6
• Early-stage disease (T1c)
• Small volume disease on biopsy
• Low PSA (< 10 ng/ml)

Active surveillance protocols include a digital rectal examination and PSA monitoring every 3 to 6 months, with TRUS-guided prostate biopsies every 1 to 3 years.

Gleason grading system evaluates the abnormalities in the glandular architecture of the prostate. It is based on a scale of 1 to 5, with 1 being the most differentiated grade and 5 being the least differentiated. The grades are added to give the Gleason score.

The classification and management of carcinoma prostate are outlined below:

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked below is innervated by which of the following motor nerve fibres?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gamma

In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked shows intrafusal muscle fibres, which are innervated by gamma(γ) motor neurons.

Each muscle spindle is 3 to 10 mm long and consists of 3 to 12 tiny intrafusal muscle fibers that are pointed at their ends and attached to the glycocalyx of the surrounding large extrafusal muscle fibers. There are two kinds of sensory endings in each spindle, a single primary (group Ia) ending and up to eight secondary (group II) endings.

Intrafusal fibers are of 2 types: (1) nuclear bag fibers - subdivided as dynamic and static nuclear bag fibers and (2) nuclear chain fibers.

Each intrafusal muscle fiber is a tiny skeletal muscle fiber. Since there are either few or no actin and myosin filaments in the centre of each of these fibres, the centre does not contract when the ends do. It performs the role of a sensory receptor instead. The end portions that do contract are excited by small gamma(γ) motor nerve fibers which help control basic muscle tone.

There are two types of γ motor neurons- (a) dynamic that supplies dynamic nuclear bag fibers and (b) static that supply static nuclear bag fibers and nuclear chain fibers.

Other options:

Option B: Alpha (α) motor fibers supply the extrafusal muscle fibers which are the regular contractile units of the muscle. They are on an average 14 micrometers in diameter and these fibers branch many times after they enter the muscle and innervate the large skeletal muscle fibers at the motor endplate. A single alpha nerve fibre can stimulate anywhere between three to several hundred skeletal muscle fibres, which are collectively called the motor unit.

Option C: Beta (β) motor fibers are for touch and pressure.

Option D: Delta (δ) motor fibers are for pain and temperature.
questions.learning: Gamma — In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked shows intrafusal muscle fibres, which are innervated by gamma(γ) motor neurons.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Periodic acid Schiff positive macrophages are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Whipple's disease

Periodic acid Schiff (PAS) positive macrophages are seen in Whipple's disease.

Whipple's disease is a chronic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, classically presents as chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, intermittent fever, weight loss, arthralgia/arthritis with neurological(cognitive changes progressing to dementia, personality and mood alterations, hypothalamic involvement and supranuclear ophthalmoplegia) and cardiological involvement (endocarditis, congestive heart failure, embolic events, aneurysms).

Investigations- Intestinal biopsy showing PAS-positive diastase resistant inclusions in lamina propria, specific PCR-based diagnosis has higher sensitivity. Urine PCR is an important tool to assess the success of therapy.

Treatment- IV ceftriaxone (2 g q12h) or meropenem (2 g q8h) for 2–4 weeks and then treated with oral doxycycline, or minocycline plus hydroxy- chloroquine for at least 1 year. Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole is used as an oral alternative, but high relapses.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent Staphylococcus infections. Laboratory evaluation reveals markedly reduced levels of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE) along with a decreased number of B cells, while skin tests show a normal response to environmental antigens. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bruton's X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA) is caused by a mutation in the BTK gene, leading to a failure in B-cell maturation. Clinically, it presents as a near-total absence of mature B cells and very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes (IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE). A critical diagnostic clue is the "normal reaction to environmental antigens," which signifies that T-cell function and cellular immunity are intact. DiGeorge syndrome (Option B) involves T-cell deficiency due to thymic hypoplasia, making skin reactions abnormal. Hyper IgM syndrome (Option C) would show elevated IgM levels. Common Variable Immunodeficiency (Option D) presents similarly but usually manifests later in life, whereas XLA appears in infancy as maternal antibodies wane. Treatment requires lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy, and patients must avoid live vaccines

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 25 year old male has thoughts of cutting his fingers, he plans and imagines doing it but never actually does it. He says that his sister is influencing his thoughts. His mother reports that he has no sister, and he talks to someone who is not present in the room. Which of the following is the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thought insertion

In the above scenario, the patient is suffering from thought insertion. Thought insertion is seen in schizophrenia. The delusion of thoughts being placed into patient’s mind by someone else.

The first rank symptoms of schizophrenia described by Kurt Schneider include :

1. Hallucination:

Audible thoughts - auditory hallucinations of a person’s voice being spoken aloud.
Voices arguing or discussing - auditory hallucinations of two or more voices arguing or discussing, usually about the person experiencing the hallucination.

Voices commenting on the patient’s actions - auditory hallucinations commenting on a person’s behavior or actions.

2. Thought Phenomenon :

* Thought withdrawal -  thoughts being actively removed from a person’s mind.

* Thought insertion - thoughts inserted into a person’s mind by some external agent.

* Thought broadcasting - the sense that a person’s thoughts are experienced by others - the thoughts are made audible or may be experienced by others through telepathy.

3. Made Phenomenon:

* Made affect - feelings are imposed on that person by an external agent.

* Made impulses or drives - an impulse for action is imposed on a person by some external agent.

* Made volitional acts - a person’s actions are controlled by an external agent; the person is a passive participant in the action.

4. Delusional perception - the person attaches an abnormal significance/meaning to a normal perception, which leads to delusional interpretation.

5. Somatic passivity - tactile or visceral hallucinations that are thought to be imposed on a person's body by some external agent. These symptoms are not specific for schizophrenia and may also be present in other psychiatric disorders.

Other options:

Option A: Forced thinking is usually seen in patients with frontal lobe epilepsy.The thoughts are formed are not in the control of the patient and are distressing thoughts.

Option C: Crowding of thoughts is also seen in schizophrenia. The patient has thoughts that are too fast and excessive and unexplainable. The patient can even locate these thoughts crowding at the back of the head.

Option D: The obsessive-compulsive symptoms are not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., a drug of abuse, a medication) or another medical condition.The patient feels the need to carry out certain behaviours to get rid of these thoughts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman with a history of chronic alcohol intake and recent NSAID use for abdominal pain presents with sudden onset of severe, generalized abdominal pain. A radiograph is provided for evaluation. Based on the clinical history and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of regular alcohol and NSAID use is a major risk factor for peptic ulcer disease, which has progressed to a surgical emergency. The provided erect chest X-ray shows pneumoperitoneum, clearly visible as a crescent of "free gas under the diaphragm". This is a pathognomonic radiological sign of Hollow Viscus Perforation, most commonly involving a perforated gastric or duodenal ulcer. While ectopic pregnancy rupture (Option A) causes severe pain and hemoperitoneum, it does not release air into the abdominal cavity. Acute pancreatitis (Option B) presents with severe pain but typically lacks free air on imaging. A perforated liver abscess (Option C) can cause peritonitis but would show fluid and potentially localized gas within the liver rather than generalized pneumoperitoneum. Therefore, the combination of specific risk factors and the presence of subdiaphragmatic free air confirms a perforated hollow organ

questions.text: An underweight adolescent girl is found to have the following finding on her ocular examination. What is the WHO grade for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1B

The given image shows a Bitot spot which is a feature seen in vitamin A deficiency. According to the WHO grading of xerophthalmia, Bitot spots are classified as 1B.

Bitos spots are triangular, pearly-white or yellowish, foamy spots on the bulbar conjunctiva on either side of the cornea.

Pearl PF0046: WHO grading of Vitamin A deficiency

The term xerophthalmia is reserved to cover all the ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency.

The first symptom of xerophthalmia is nyctalopia.

The pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia is the appearance of Bitot's spots.

Up to the level of Stage 2, the manifestations are reversible if treated with vitamin A supplements.

However, active conjunctival xerosis and Bitot’s spots begin to resolve within 2—5 days after supplementation. Most will disappear within 2 weeks, although a significant proportion of temporal lesions may persist in shrunken form and may therefore not be completely reversible.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Puerperal pyrexia can be diagnosed if a woman has :
options: A temperature of >100.4 F, 12 hours after delivery
A temperature of >100.4 F, 6 hours after delivery
A temperature of >100.4 F, 24 hours after delivery
A temperature of >100.4 F, 3 hours after delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A temperature of >100.4 F, 24 hours after delivery

Puerperal fever is defined as a temperature of >100.4 °F (38 °C or higher) on 2 separate occasions at 24 hours apart (excluding the first 24 hours) within the first 10 days following delivery.

In the first 24 hours, a slight rise in temperature is not uncommon. Hence the first 24 hours are excluded to define puerperal pyrexia.

Note: Generally, fever in an adult is defined as an oral temperature of >37.5 °C.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient is started on a short-acting inhaled β2-agonist for COPD. Which of the following effects would be expected with this class of drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypokalemia

Short-acting β₂-agonists (SABAs) such as salbutamol (albuterol) produce bronchodilation by stimulating β₂-adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle. β₂ receptor activation also enhances Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, driving potassium into cells and causing hypokalemia, especially at higher doses.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hyperkalemia – β₂ agonists lower, rather than raise, serum potassium levels.
• B. Bronchoconstriction – β₂ stimulation causes bronchodilation.
• D. Pulmonary vasoconstriction– β₂ agonists generally promote smooth muscle relaxation, not vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following channels is defective in a child with a CFTR gene defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cl-

A child with a CFTR(Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein) mutation will have cystic fibrosis. Abnormalities in the CFTR gene lead to defective chloride (Cl-) channels.

Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, digestive system, and other organs. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which leads to the production of thick and sticky mucus. The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include:

* Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps.

* Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis.

* Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels.

* Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females.

* Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease.

Diagnostic tests:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

1. Presence of

* Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or

* Positive newborn screening or

* A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

* Two positive sweat chloride test results were obtained on separate days or

* Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or

* An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference.

Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.
questions.learning: Cl- — A child with a CFTR(Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein) mutation will have cystic fibrosis. Abnormalities in the CFTR gene lead to defective chloride (Cl-) channels.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true about febrile seizure?
options: Simple febrile seizure lasts for <15 minutes
No need for long term antiepileptics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 54% recurrence

Febrile seizures are benign, age-dependent seizures occurring in children between 6 months and 5 years in association with fever, without evidence of intracranial infection or metabolic cause.

• Simple febrile seizures are generalized, last less than 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours
• Long-term antiepileptic therapy is not indicated due to the benign nature and low risk of epilepsy
• Recurrence risk is about 30–35%, not as high as 54%

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic presents with agitation, global confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, fever, hypertension, diaphoresis, and autonomic hyperactivity after 48 hours of alcohol cessation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's clinical presentation of agitation, global confusion, and autonomic hyperactivity (fever, hypertension, diaphoresis) starting 48 hours after the cessation of alcohol is the hallmark of Delirium Tremens (DT). DT is the most severe manifestation of alcohol withdrawal and is a medical emergency. Wernicke Encephalopathy (Option B) presents with the triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia due to thiamine deficiency. Korsakoff Psychosis (Option C) is a chronic memory disorder following Wernicke's, characterized by confabulation. Magnan Phenomena (Option D), or formication, is a sensory hallucination of crawling insects that can occur within the context of DT but is not the diagnosis itself. DT requires aggressive treatment with benzodiazepines and intravenous fluids to prevent cardiovascular collapse and death. Its high mortality rate necessitates immediate hospitalization in an intensive care setting for close monitoring of vital signs and neurological status
questions.learning: The patient's clinical presentation of agitation, global confusion, and autonomic hyperactivity (fever, hypertension, diaphoresis) starting 48 hours after the cessation of alcohol is the hallmark of Delirium Tremens (DT).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female presents with hirsutism, delayed periods & obesity. USG findings are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome

The given clinical scenario and the ultrasound image given below showing an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery(a string of pearls) is indicative of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS).

PCOS is an endocrinopathy seen in women of reproductive age, affecting multiple systems. The Rotterdam criteria are used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS:

* Clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne)

* Menstrual abnormalities (oligo/amenorrhoea), anovulation, infertility

* Polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography.

Sonographic criteria for polycystic ovaries include ≥ 12 small cysts, an increased ovarian volume (> 10 mL) or both.

Management:

* Weight reduction alone is beneficial in mild hirsutism and lifestyle changes (like smoking cessation) are advised in the management of PCOS.

* Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. It also reduces acne and further hirsutism.

* Anti-androgens are useful in treating hirsutism. OCP with cyproterone acetate is prescribed for PCOS patients with hirsutism.

* Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin. Acarbose can be used if metformin is contraindicated

* Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole.

Surgical options include laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. This is done either by laser or by unipolar electrocautery. It restores the endocrine levels and improves fertility.

Surgery is indicated only if,

* Medical therapy fails

* Hyperstimulation occurs

* Infertile women

* Previous pregnancy losses

Other Options:

Option B: Molar Pregnancy will produce a characteristic Snowstorm appearance on ultrasound.

Option C: Enlarged ovaries meeting in the midline having large cysts are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Option D: The image below depicts multiple theca lutein cysts.

Pearl PF1877: Endocrinological changes of PCOD

* Elevated Estrone/E1 levels.

* LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls.

* Testosterone and epi-androstenedione levels rise.

* Testosterone elevated but < 200 ng/dL (normal range 20 - 70 ng/dL)

* Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests androgen-secreting ovarian tumor

* DHEA-S values may be normal or slightly elevated

* DHEA >700 ng/mL suggests adrenal tumour

* Serum SHBG is reduced.

* Triglyceride level >150 mg/dL-hyperlipidaemia HDL <50 mg/dL.

* Fasting blood glucose/fasting insulin <4.5 suggests insulin resistance

* Prolactin is mildly raised in 15% cases

* Fasting insulin is more than 10 mIU/L in PCOS in 50–70%cases

* Thyroid function tests may be abnormal (hypothyroidism)

* 17-a-hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase >300 ng/dL suggests adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

* Urinary cortisol <50 μg/24 h.

Pearl PF1729: Management of PCOD

Complaint
Management

Irregular periods
OCPs

Obesity
Lifestyle modification

Insulin resistance
Metformin

Hirsutism /acne
OCPs with cyproterone acetate

Infertility
Clomiphene

Note: Letrozole is as effective as Clomiphene in treating infertility in PCOD with fewer side effects. However, it's pending FDA approval and is used off-label.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown below?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates Condyloma acuminata, commonly known as genital warts. These are caused by infection with low-risk strains of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV), most frequently types 6 and 11. They characteristically appear as fleshy, "cauliflower-like," or filiform exophytic growths on the skin and mucous membranes of the anogenital region. In contrast, condyloma lata (Option A) are a manifestation of secondary syphilis and appear as broad, flat, moist papules that are highly infectious. Molluscum contagiosum (Option C) is caused by a poxvirus and presents as small, discrete, umbilicated pearly papules. Condyloma acuminata is a highly contagious sexually transmitted infection. Management includes topical therapies like podophyllin or imiquimod, or destructive methods such as cryotherapy, electrocautery, or laser excision. Prevention is primarily through the HPV vaccine, which covers these common low-risk strains. Accurate clinical differentiation between these conditions is essential, as the underlying etiologies and necessary pharmacological treatments (antivirals/cryotherapy vs. penicillin for syphilis) differ significantly

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Name the drug that acts on both the marked points.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Omapatrilat

Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System (RAAS) and the natriuretic peptide degradation pathway

Two key enzymes are involved:

| Enzyme | Function

| ------ | --------

| ACE (Angiotensin Converting Enzyme) | Converts Ang I → Ang II

| Neprilysin | Breaks down natriuretic peptides

If a drug blocks both these points, it inhibits:

• ACE
• Neprilysin

The marked points represent ACE and neutral endopeptidase (NEP).

Omapatrilat is a vasopeptidase inhibitor that simultaneously inhibits ACE and NEP.

This reduces angiotensin II while increasing natriuretic peptides and bradykinin.

Sacubitril inhibits only NEP, losartan blocks AT₁ receptors, and nesiritide is a BNP analogue.

A) Sacubitril

Only neprilysin inhibitor, not ACE inhibitor.

C) Losartan

An ARB, blocks angiotensin II receptor only.

D) Nesiritide

Recombinant BNP, causes vasodilation but does not inhibit enzymes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Osimertinib is used in NSCLC with which of the following mutation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. T790M mutation

The T790M mutation in the EGFR gene is known to cause resistance to first and second-generation EGFR inhibitors. Osimertinib, as a third-generation EGFR inhibitor, is effective against this resistance, hence it is often used for patients with the T790M mutation after they've progressed on first or second-generation EGFR inhibitors.

The question seems to be asking specifically for the mutation that osimertinib is particularly known for being used against, and that would be the T790M mutation.

Osimertinib is a kinase inhibitor that is approved for

• Patients with metastatic non small cell lung carcinoma(NSCLC) that has progressed after prior EGFR TKI treatment and is positive for the EGFR T790M mutation.
• First-line treatment of patients with metastatic NSCLC and adjuvant therapy after resection of NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R mutations

So, osimertinib is used both for the L858R mutation and T790M mutation in different settings. But T790M mutation is often highlighted because of its association with resistance to first and second-generation EGFR inhibitors, and because osimertinib can overcome this resistance.

Osimertinib is administered orally and is a substrate of CYP3A. The drug is primarily eliminated in the feces and to a lesser extent in the urine. Concurrent administration of inducers of CYP3A4 may necessitate an increase in the dose.

The adverse effects after osimertinib treatment are leukopenia, diarrhea, skin rash, interstitial lung disease, QTc prolongation, and left ventricular dysfunction.
