questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which among the following is not used in post laryngectomy rehabilitation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Super supraglottic swallow

Super supraglottic swallow is not used in post-laryngectomy rehabilitation.

Super-supraglottic swallow is a maneuver that prevents the aspiration of food or liquid by closing the airway before swallowing. It is used in the management of dysphagia. This method involves holding one’s breath to close the airway prior to swallowing, followed by coughing voluntarily immediately after swallowing to clear any residual food or liquid from the airway entrance. It is an effortful breath-holding technique, which not only results in Valsalva and subsequent leakage of bolus but can also result in arrhythmias.

Other options:

Option A: A tracheoesophageal prosthesis(TEP) involves a one-way valve that is inserted through a previously-created tracheoesophageal puncture. When the patient occludes the stoma, the exhaled air is shunted through the TEP into the oesophagus, where it induces vibration of the upper oesophagal sphincter, which is responsible for phonation. It generates the most intelligible, fluent, natural-sounding voice in contrast to other laryngeal speech methods.

Option B: Oesophagal speech also involves vibration of the upper oesophagal sphincter and subsequent phonation.

Option C: Polite yawning also called the nasal airflow-inducing maneuver is an important olfaction rehabilitation tool after a laryngectomy.

Electrolarynx produces vibrations that are transmitted through the skin toward the throat. The sound generated is converted into low-pitch speech by the vocal tract—palate, tongue, and teeth. The advantages are that is easy and quick to learn, while the disadvantages are that the voice is monotonous and the constant occupation of one hand.
questions.learning: Super supraglottic swallow Super supraglottic swallow is not used in post-laryngectomy rehabilitation. Super-supraglottic swallow is a maneuver that prevents the aspiration of food or liquid by closing the airway before swallowing.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Silent choroid on FFA is a feature of which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stargardt's disease

Silent/Dark choroid on FFA is a feature of Stargardt's disease. The classic feature of 'silent choroid' is due to the masking of background choroidal fluorescence by lipofuscin deposits in the subretinal space.

Stargardt disease constitutes the most common type of macular dystrophy. It has mutations in a photoreceptor cell-specific ATP-binding cassette gene (ABC4) that is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The disease usually starts in the juvenile group with progressive central vision loss and color vision loss that occurs due to the atrophy of the macular retinal pigment epithelium with an accumulation of discrete pisciform flecks of lipofuscin.

Signs of Stargardt’s disease:

• Beaten bronze appearance of the macula that is caused by the atrophic changes in the RPE.
• Silent/Dark choroid on FFA.
• Visual field testing shows central vision loss.
• The electroretinogram (ERG) is normal early in the disease but may be reduced in more advanced cases.

Fundus flavimaculatus is genetically considered to be a part of the same spectrum as Stargardt's disease with late onset i.e. usually after 40 years of age.

Other options:

Option B: Best's disease also known as vitelliform macular dystrophy is an autosomal dominant macular dystrophy in which lipofuscin accumulates in the central macula, causing progressive central vision loss. This disease is linked to mutations in the bestrophin (VMD2) gene and they do not exhibit silent choroid on FFA. Findings seen in Best’s disease are:

• Vitelliform(yolk like) appearance of the fundus
• Relatively normal ERG results associated with abnormal EOG

The given below is the fundus picture of Best's disease showing an egg yolk lesion in the macula.

Option C: Age related Macular degeneration(ARMD) also known as senile macular degeneration is a chronic and progressive bilateral degenerative disorder of the macula that affects older individuals >50 yrs. ARMD is classified as dry and wet ARMD where the hallmarks are the presence of drusen and choroidal neovascularization respectively. Drusen are extracellular eosinophilic deposits between RPE and Bruch’s membrane.

Clinical features include loss of central vision, distorted vision (lines seen as wavy), and sudden painless loss of vision as seen in wet ARMD. The image below shows Drusens in the macular area in dry macular degeneration.

Option D: Cystoid Macular edema (CME) is a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform layer and the inner nuclear layer of the retina following a break in the blood-retinal barrier. In CME on fundoscopy, a honeycomb appearance and on FFA flower petal pattern can be seen. The below image shows the flower petal pattern on FFA as seen in CME.
questions.learning: Stargardt's disease Silent/Dark choroid on FFA is a feature of Stargardt's disease. The classic feature of 'silent choroid' is due to the masking of background choroidal fluorescence by lipofuscin deposits in the subretinal space.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following refractive errors is associated with the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Astigmatism

The given image is a Sturm's conoid. It represents the configuration of a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic (toric) surface and helps in understanding the optics of regular astigmatism.

Astigmatism is a type of refractive error that occurs when light rays enter the eye at different planes and converge at different points forming focal lines.

When light passes through a regularly astigmatic surface (surface with toric curvature), vertical and horizontal rays converge at different points and form two focal lines. The shape of a bundle of light rays at different points is as follows:

For the given Sturm's conoid,

• At point A, a horizontal oval is formed because vertical rays converge more rapidly than horizontal rays.
• At point B (first focus), vertical rays come to a focus, while horizontal rays are still converging; so, it will be a horizontal straight line.
• At points C, D, and E, the vertical rays are diverging, and horizontal rays are still converging.
• At point D, the vertical rays have diverged as much as the horizontal rays have converged; so, we get a perfect circle called the circle of least diffusion.
• At point E, a vertical oval is formed.
• At point F (second focus), a vertical straight line is formed
• At point G and beyond, both rays are diverging, and we always get a vertical oval/ prolate ellipse.
• The focal interval of Sturm refers to the distance between two foci (B and F).

The image is clearest or least confusing as point D, the circle of least confusion/ circle of diffusion. The circle of diffusion lies at the mid-point of this interval.

• Option A: Presbyopia is a refractive error caused by the loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens, leading to difficulty in focusing on near objects. Presbyopia is not associated with Sturm's conoid.
• Option C: Hypermetropia, or farsightedness, is a refractive error in which the eye does not focus incoming light properly, causing near objects to appear blurry. It is not associated with Sturm's conoid.
• Option D: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a refractive error in which distant objects appear blurry because the eye focuses light in front of the retina rather than on it. Myopia is not associated with Sturm's conoid.
questions.learning: Astigmatism — The given image is a Sturm's conoid. It represents the configuration of a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic (toric) surface and helps in understanding the optics of regular astigmatism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presented with diffuse abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed rigidity and guarding. Abdominal X-ray demonstrated free air under the diaphragm. The patient was taken up for surgery and intraoperatively, ileal perforation was noted with gross contamination of the abdomen with enteric and purulent content. What is the appropriate management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent surgical exploration with ileostomy

The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggest peritonitis due to perforation. The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration with an ileostomy.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. Common causes include iatrogenic (surgery, scopes) blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, infections( TB, typhoid) peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications

This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation.

Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are

* Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient)

* Bowel ischemia

* Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction

Other options:

Option A: Resection is considered in a patient with multiple perforation, suspected gangrene or malignancy. Anastomosis is avoided in patients in shock, peritonitis with gross contamination

Option B: Primary repair is usually taken for small perforation with minimal contamination and no sign of peritonitis. It is commonly done for traumatic enteric perforation

Option D: Duodenal perforations, on the other hand, are generally treated with omental patch repair without resection.
questions.learning: Urgent surgical exploration with ileostomy — The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggest peritonitis due to perforation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is biopsied for the diagnosis of pure neuritic leprosy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superficial branch of radial nerve

Superficial sensory branch of the radial nerve is most commonly used for nerve biopsy in neuritic leprosy.

Although any nerve involved would show the pathology, it is prudent to biopsy a branch of a sensory nerve, rather than a mixed nerve or major nerve trunk. So, the ulnar nerve will not be the best answer despite it being the most common peripheral nerve involved in neuritic leprosy.

The common nerves and sites where nerve biopsy is performed in leprosy are as follows:

• Superficial sensory radial nerve branch at the wrist
• Ulnar cutaneous nerve near the ulnar border of the base of the hand
• Sural nerve near the ankle

Note: Nerve biopsy is the gold standard for confirmation of pure neuritic leprosy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In Pap smear cytology, which of the following is the most appropriate fixative used to preserve cellular details immediately after smearing?
questions.explanation: For a conventional Pap smear, immediate fixation is critical to stabilize cellular structures and prevent air-drying artifacts. The standard fixative used is 95% ethanol, which works by precipitating proteins and maintaining the life-like appearance of the cells for microscopic examination. Formaldehyde (Options A and D) is a cross-linking fixative most commonly used for whole tissue preservation in histology but is not the primary fixative for cytological smears. 70% ethanol (Option C) is generally used as a disinfectant rather than a cytology fixative. Cells are collected from the cervical transformation zone, smeared onto a slide, and immediately immersed in or sprayed with 95% ethanol. This ensures the precise detail of the nucleus and cytoplasm is preserved for cancer screening

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted on workers in an aniline dye factory. One group consisted of workers exposed to the dye, and the other group included clerical staff with no exposure. All relevant information was collected from factory records spanning the past 20 years. What type of study does this represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retrospective study

Factory workers exposed to aniline dye were compared with clerical staff using records from the past 20 years. Since both the exposure and outcomes had already occurred, and the study moved forward from those past records to analyze disease occurrence, it points towards a retrospective cohort study.

A cohort study progresses from cause (exposure) to effect (disease).

* Types of cohort study:

* Prospective (concurrent) cohort studies

* Retrospective (historical) cohort studies

* Combination cohort studies

* Steps of cohort study:

* Selection of study subjects

* Obtaining data on exposure

* Selection of comparison groups

* Follow-up

* Analysis in terms of incidence rates and estimation of risk

* Advantages of cohort study:

* Incidence can be calculated

* Several possible outcomes related to exposure can be studied at the same time

* Provides direct estimate of relative risk

* Calculation of dose-response ratio

* Minimization of certain biases

* Disadvantages of cohort study:

* Cannot use for uncommon diseases

* Expensive, requires a large population and longer time

* Many common administrative and ethical problems

* High attrition and selection of subjects is difficult

* Dynamism of diagnostics is difficult to incorporate

* Tends to alter the behaviour of subjects known as Hawthorne effect.

Other options:

Option A: In a case-control study, the study begins with the outcome and goes retrospectively to find out the exposure among the cases and controls.For example, to find the exposure to smoking associated with already diagnosed lung cancer patients.

Option B: An ecological study is any kind of study in which data is collected about a population and is analyzed at that level. Unlike the case with cohort studies, in these studies, no data is available or analyzed about individuals.

Option D: A cross-sectional study Is an observational study used to calculate a disease's distribution and prevalence.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the homunculus, which of the following has maximum representation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased preciseness of movements

In a homunculus, the more the representation of an area, the more precise the movements are.

• The relative sizes of the cortical receiving areas of the sensory homunculus are proportionate to the use of the part.
• The sizes of these areas are directly proportional to the number of specialized sensory receptors in each respective peripheral area of the body.
• Some body parts are represented by large areas in the somatic cortex—the lips the greatest of all, followed by the face and thumb, whereas the trunk and lower part of the body are represented by relatively small areas.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the management of shoulder dystocia during childbirth, which maneuver is typically attempted first as the initial step?
questions.explanation: The McRoberts maneuver is the critical first-line physical intervention for managing shoulder dystocia. It involves hyperflexing the mother's thighs against her abdomen. This action flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the symphysis pubis superiorly, increasing the space available for the anterior shoulder to pass under the pelvic bone. Rotational maneuvers like the Rubin (Option C) and Woods corkscrew (Option B) are performed only if simpler measures like McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail. Delivery of the posterior arm (Option D) is an internal maneuver attempted later in the algorithm. Because of its high success rate and relative simplicity, the McRoberts maneuver is the mandated starting point in emergency shoulder dystocia protocols
questions.learning: The McRoberts maneuver is the critical first-line physical intervention for managing shoulder dystocia. It involves hyperflexing the mother's thighs against her abdomen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A tall obese person, who is a known hypertensive was recently diagnosed with metabolic syndrome on routine workup. Which of the following is most likely to be found in this patient?
options: Increase in uric acid and insulin
Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol

Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol is seen in patients with metabolic syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome is present if three or more of the following five criteria are met, which is given by NCEP-ATP III (National Cholesterol Education program and adult treatment panel III). It includes-

* Central obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (M), >88 cm (F)

* Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥ 150 mg/dL

* Low HDL cholesterol: <40 mg/dL and <50 mg/dL for men and women, respectively.

* Hypertension: blood pressure ≥130 mmHg systolic or ≥ 85 mmHg diastolic.

* Fasting plasma glucose level ≥100 mg/dL or specific medication or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol is seen in patients with metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is present if three or more of the following five criteria are met, which is given by NCEP-ATP…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient complains of frequent episodes of red, painful eyes, stiffness, and back pain. He has sacroiliitis and anterior uveitis, according to the examination. Which HLA is frequently involved among the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HLA B27

| Clue | Interpretation

| ---- | --------------

| Young adult (35 yrs) | Typical age group

| Chronic back pain + stiffness | Inflammatory back pain

| Sacroiliitis | Hallmark of spondyloarthropathy

| Anterior uveitis (red painful eye) | Extra-articular feature

Diagnosis points to: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS)

And the genetic association:  HLA-B27

HLA-B27 is like a genetic “ID card” for spondyloarthropathies:

• Present in \~90–95% of ankylosing spondylitis
• Associated with:

• Reactive arthritis
• Psoriatic arthritis
• Enteropathic arthritis

• Chronic inflammation at entheses (ligament insertions)
• Leads to:

• Fibrosis
• Ossification

• Spine becomes rigid → “Bamboo spine”

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient falls onto an outstretched hand, and an X-ray shows a fracture of the first metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint with associated subluxation. How is this type of fracture classified?
questions.explanation: The X-ray and clinical description define a Bennett's fracture, which is an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. It typically occurs due to axial loading on a partially flexed thumb, such as from a fall on an outstretched hand. The fracture involves a small fragment of the metacarpal base remaining attached to the volar oblique ligament, while the main metacarpal shaft is subluxed proximally and dorsally by the pull of the abductor pollicis longus (APL) muscle. Scaphoid fractures (Option B) involve the carpal bones and are noted for pain in the anatomical snuffbox. Colle's fracture (Option D) is a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement ("dinner fork" deformity), while Reverse Colle's (Smith's fracture, Option C) involves volar displacement of the distal radius. Because this fracture specifically involves the base of the thumb's metacarpal with subluxation, it is identified as a Bennett's fracture
questions.learning: The X-ray and clinical description define a Bennett's fracture, which is an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. It typically occurs due to axial loading on a partially flexed thumb, such as from a fall on an outstretched hand.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: How should steroid therapy be administered for a 55-year-old male diagnosed with Addison's disease?
options: Bolus of 100mg, followed by 200mg over 24 hours
Bolus of 200 mg, followed by 500 mg over 24 hours
questions.explanation: In the management of an Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency), rapid replacement of glucocorticoids is life-saving. The standard protocol involves an immediate intravenous bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone. This is followed by either continuous infusion or intermittent doses totaling 200 mg over the subsequent 24 hours. Options C and D (500 mg) represent excessively high doses that are generally not required and increase the risk of side effects. Hydrocortisone is preferred because it has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, though aggressive fluid resuscitation with normal saline is also mandatory to correct the associated hypotension and electrolyte imbalances (hyponatremia/hyperkalemia). Once the patient is stabilized and can tolerate oral intake, the dose is gradually tapered to a maintenance level (typically 15–25 mg daily). Identifying the trigger for the crisis, such as infection or stress, is also a critical part of management to prevent future life-threatening episodes
questions.learning: In the management of an Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency), rapid replacement of glucocorticoids is life-saving. The standard protocol involves an immediate intravenous bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which test is used to differentiate human blood from the blood of other animal species?
questions.explanation: In forensic medicine, several tests are used to analyze blood stains. The Precipitin test is specifically designed to determine if a blood sample is of human origin or from another species. It utilizes an antiserum containing antibodies that react specifically with human serum proteins, creating a visible precipitate. Teichman (Option A) and Takayama (Option D) tests are confirmatory tests used to identify the presence of blood by forming characteristic hemin or hemochromogen crystals, but they cannot distinguish between species. The Barberio test (Option C) is a forensic test used for the identification of semen (spermine) rather than blood. Therefore, while several tests confirm that a substance is indeed blood, the Precipitin test is the only one among the choices capable of verifying its species-specific origin, making it essential for criminal investigations involving blood evidence
questions.learning: In forensic medicine, several tests are used to analyze blood stains. The Precipitin test is specifically designed to determine if a blood sample is of human origin or from another species.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with vomiting and diarrhea occurring about 20 minutes after meals following a Billroth II gastrectomy. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this condition?
options: Conversion of Billroth II to Billroth I procedure
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing Early Dumping Syndrome, a common complication following gastric surgeries like a Billroth II gastrectomy. It results from the rapid delivery of hyperosmolar food into the small intestine, leading to fluid shifts and vasomotor symptoms. The most appropriate initial management involves dietary modification, specifically eating small, frequent meals and avoiding large amounts of simple carbohydrates. Patients should also be advised to separate solid food and liquid intake (avoiding drinking with meals). A low-fat diet (Option A) is not the primary focus for dumping. Insulin (Option C) would worsen the hypoglycemia seen in late dumping. Surgical conversion (Option D) is a last resort reserved only for severe cases refractory to all medical and dietary management. Most patients achieve significant symptomatic relief by simply changing their eating habits to slow the transit of food into the jejunum. These dietary adjustments are the cornerstone of post-gastrectomy care

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He was unable to pass urine and blood was seen at the tip of the urethra. A diagnosis of bulbar urethral injury was made. Where do you least expect the urine to get collected in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial portion of thigh

In bulbar urethral injury, the medial portion of the thigh is the least likely site for the collection of urine.

The rupture of the urethra below the urogenital diaphragm will result in extravasation of urine into the superficial perineal pouch, penis and scrotum in males and labia majora in females, and the anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial fascia of the abdomen is divided below the umbilicus into a superficial fatty layer (fascia of Camper) and a deep membranous layer (fascia of Scarpa). Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the membranous layer of the superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia).

Colles' fascia is attached to fascia lata (the deep fascia of the thigh) along the Holden's line that extends from the pubic tubercle laterally for 8 cm. Extravasated fluid cannot pass into the medial thigh below Holden's line due to the firm attachment of Colles' fascia to the fascia lata.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic man presents with altered consciousness, disorientation and severe agitation. He reports his last alcohol intake was 48 hours ago. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The clinical scenario of a 45-year-old chronic alcoholic man with altered consciousness, disorientation and severe agitation and his last alcohol consumption 48 hours ago points to delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are:

* Altered sensorium with disorientation

* Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations

* Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, and hypertension. And sweating

* Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy
Altered sleep-wake cycle

Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterised by:

* Global confusion

* Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex

* Ataxia—mainly affecting the gait

* Vestibular dysfunction

It may resolve with thiamine therapy or progress to Korsakoff's syndrome.

Other options:

Option B: Alcohol-induced psychosis is a severe mental condition triggered by excessive alcohol use, leading to hallucinations, delusions, and confusion. It typically occurs during withdrawal or chronic alcohol abuse and requires immediate medical intervention.

Option C: Opioid withdrawal can cause symptoms like drug craving, feelings of temperature change, musculoskeletal pain, and GI distress. Signs of opioid withdrawal include confusion, drowsiness, vomiting, and diarrhoea. It is not typically life-threatening, especially compared to alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, which can lead to seizures or delirium tremens. Hence, opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal.

Option D: Alcohol-induced hallucinations occur due to excessive alcohol use or withdrawal, causing false visual, auditory, or tactile perceptions. They are distinct from delirium tremens and can persist even with clear consciousness.

Pearl PF1275: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome

Manifestation

Symptoms/signs

Onset since last drink (hours)

Tremulousness

Continuous tremor of > 8 Hz (or) Bursts of tremor activity < 8 Hz

6–8

Alcoholic hallucinosis/

Psychotic and perceptual symptoms

Visual, auditory or tactile; intact orientation; stable vital signs.

8-12

Seizures (rum fits)

Single or multiple generalized tonic-clonic

12–24

Delirium tremens

Confusion, agitation, fever, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, impaired orientation

< 72
questions.learning: Delirium tremens — The clinical scenario of a 45-year-old chronic alcoholic man with altered consciousness, disorientation and severe agitation and his last alcohol consumption 48 hours ago points to delirium tremens.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following condition is depicted in the given CT image?
questions.explanation: (CAH) The CT image shows bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with a lobulated / cerebriform appearance, which is a classic radiological finding of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. In CAH, chronic ACTH stimulation leads to diffuse adrenal hyperplasia, typically involving both adrenal glands symmetrically. Why the other options are incorrect (A) HCC (Hepatocellular carcinoma) – Would show a focal liver mass with arterial enhancement and washout, not bilateral adrenal enlargement. (B) Hepatitis – Causes diffuse liver changes, not adrenal enlargement. (D) Cirrhosis – Shows a shrunken, nodular liver with portal hypertension features (splenomegaly, ascites), not this appearance
questions.learning: (CAH) The CT image shows bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with a lobulated / cerebriform appearance, which is a classic radiological finding of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 16-month-old boy is found to weigh 8kg. A WHO growth chart(weight-for-age) is provided below. Plot the growth chart for this child. What is the most appropriate advice based on the plotted graph?
options: Severe malnutrition - refer to nutrition rehabilitation center
Moderate malnutrition - teach the mother on how to feed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Moderate malnutrition - teach the mother on how to feed

The weight for age of the child falls in between -2SD and -3SD as shown in the growth chart below, which is suggestive of moderate malnutrition and the mother should be taught to feed the baby properly.

The primary treatment in mild and moderate malnutrition involves providing sufficient protein and energy intake, with a recommended minimum of 150 kcal/kg/day. Nutritious home food is advised, and frequent feeding (up to 7 times a day) may be required to achieve the necessary energy intake. High-fat foods are often used to increase energy in therapeutic diets.

Animal-source foods, such as milk and eggs, are recommended by WHO as they provide necessary amino acids and nutrients. Plant-source foods like legumes and cereals can also be good protein sources. A slight increase in protein intake (3g/kg/day) is sufficient for catch-up growth with high energy intake. Milk and vegetable protein mixtures can be used as a protein source and adequate minerals and vitamins are also added.

Weight gain is the best measure of treatment efficacy for mild and moderate malnutrition.

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) should be referred to a hospital for proper management. Uncomplicated SAM can be managed at home under supervision. Complicated SAM should be treated as an inpatient.

Management of SAM is summarized in the image below.

The World Health Organization(WHO) has established international standards for normal child growth from birth to 5 years of age. The normalization of the anthropometric measures is done in terms of z-scores (standard deviation scores). The anthropometric indicators are marked in a growth chart which is compared with a reference curve.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

• Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.
• High weight-for-height indicates overweight.
• Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
• Low weight for the age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is used for the screening of wasting in children between 6 months to 5 years. In children aged 6 months to 5 years, MUAC <11.5cm is considered as severe malnutrition.
questions.learning: Moderate malnutrition - teach the mother on how to feed The weight for age of the child falls in between -2SD and -3SD as shown in the growth chart below, which is suggestive of moderate malnutrition and the mother should be taught to feed the baby properly.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman at 18 weeks of gestation undergoes routine antenatal screening. Her random plasma glucose is elevated, subsequent fasting blood glucose is raised, and her HbA1c level is 7.6%. Based on these laboratory findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Maturity onset diabetes of the young
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of diabetes during pregnancy is categorized based on the timing and severity of hyperglycemia. "Overt diabetes" (or pre-gestational diabetes) is diagnosed when criteria for non-pregnant diabetes are met during the first prenatal visit or early pregnancy. The patient’s HbA1c of 7.6% and fasting glucose of clearly exceed the diagnostic thresholds (HbA1c 6.5% or fasting glucose ). Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM, Option C) is typically diagnosed between 24–28 weeks using less stringent thresholds and represents glucose intolerance that begins during pregnancy. Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY, Option A) and Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA, Option D) are specific types of diabetes defined by genetics or antibodies, but the immediate clinical classification for this pregnant woman is overt diabetes. Patients with overt diabetes have a higher risk of congenital anomalies and require intensive glycemic management throughout the pregnancy to ensure optimal maternal and neonatal outcomes

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of chest pain which is seen only on exertion or exercise and lasts 2-5 minutes. He was assessed and was diagnosed with a case of stable angina however his BP was consistently elevated. What is the most appropriate antihypertensive for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atenolol

The antihypertensive drug of choice in stable angina is beta-blockers which is atenolol here.

Atenolol is a cardioselective beta-blocker that works by decreasing cardiac contractility and heart rate which decreases cardiac output and blood pressure.

Beta-blockers are also used in congestive cardiac failure which has been shown to decrease their mortality rates.

Stable angina:

* Stable angina is caused by an imbalance in coronary perfusion (due to chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis) relative to myocardial demand.

* Squeezing, central, substernal discomfort

* Crescendo-decrescendo in nature

* Typically lasts 2 to 5 min

* Can radiate to either shoulder & to both arms (especially the ulnar surfaces of the forearm & hand)

* It also can arise in or radiate to the back, interscapular region, the root of the neck, jaw, teeth, and epigastrium.

Other types of angina

* Prinzmetal variant angina is an uncommon form of episodic myocardial ischemia; it is caused by coronary artery spasm.

* Unstable or crescendo angina refers to a pattern of increasingly frequent, prolonged (>20 min), or severe angina or chest discomfort that is described as frank pain, precipitated by progressively lower levels of physical activity or even occurring at rest.

Pearl PF0731: Anti-anginal drugs

Anti-anginal drugs can be divided into the following categories:

* Nitrates - Dilates veins > arteries. Reduces preload.

* Calcium channel blockers - Blocks L-type calcium channels

* Dihydropyridines - Amlodipine, nifedipine

* Non-dihydropyridines - Verapamil, Diltiazem

* Beta-blockers - Decreases heart rate, contractility and oxygen demand

* Other drugs

* Ranolazine - Late Na+ channel blocker

* Ivabradine - Inhibit funny currents in SA node

* Nicorandil - K+-ATP channel agonist

* Trimetazidine - pFOX inhibitor

* Fasudil - Rho-kinase inhibitor
questions.learning: Atenolol — The antihypertensive drug of choice in stable angina is beta-blockers which is atenolol here. Atenolol is a cardioselective beta-blocker that works by decreasing cardiac contractility and heart rate which decreases cardiac output and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He gets an urge to micturate but is unable to urinate. On examination, blood was seen at the tip of the urethra, and swelling of the penis and scrotum was seen. What is the site of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulbar urethra injury

The given clinical scenario with a history of a blow to the perineum, blood at the tip of the meatus, swelling of the penis and scrotum is suggestive of an injury to the bulbar urethra.

Urethral injuries can be classified into:

Type
Proximal urethral injury
Distal urethral injury

Site of injury

• Prostatic urethra
• Membranous urethra

• Bulbar urethra
• Penile urethra

Mechanism
Secondary to pelvic fracture

Occurs due to a blow to the perineum by:

• Straddle injury
• Loose manhole covering
• Gymnasium accidents

Clinical features

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)
• Deep perineal hematoma

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• Perineal hematoma (butterfly hematoma)

Note: Urinary bladder rupture occurs due to an injury to the suprapubic region. Extraperitoneal bladder rupture is more common and associated with pelvic fracture. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture is caused by a blow or a fall on a distended bladder. It manifests as sudden severe pain in the hypogastrium and syncope.
questions.learning: Bulbar urethra injury — The given clinical scenario with a history of a blow to the perineum, blood at the tip of the meatus, swelling of the penis and scrotum is suggestive of an injury to the bulbar urethra.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with sudden onset severe headache and vomiting. On examination, he has neck stiffness. A CT scan of the brain shows hydrocephalus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

The classic triad here is:

• Sudden onset severe headache ("thunderclap headache" — worst headache of life)
• Neck stiffness (meningeal irritation)
• Young patient (20-year-old)

This points strongly to SAH, most commonly caused by rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm.

Why the other options are wrong

| Option | Why eliminated

| ------ | --------------

| A - Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus | Occurs in elderly with classic triad: dementia, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence — not sudden headache

| B - Bacterial Meningitis | Can cause neck stiffness, but headache is gradual, fever is prominent, and CT rarely shows hydrocephalus acutely

| C - Viral Encephalitis | Presents with altered consciousness, fever, seizures — not sudden thunderclap headache

Key Exam Points

• SAH = "worst headache of life" + neck stiffness + young patient
• CT shows hyperdense (white) blood in basal cisterns
• If CT negative → do lumbar puncture (xanthochromia)
• Most common cause: berry aneurysm (Circle of Willis)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted on two different samples for comparing variation between DBP and Vitamin D. The mean diastolic blood pressure is 110 with standard deviation 11 and the mean vitamin D level is 18 with standard deviation 3. Which of the following statement is true regarding the coefficient of variation (CV)?
options: CV of DBP is more than Vitamin D
CV of Vitamin D is more than DBP
Both DBP and Vitamin D have equal variability
It cannot be ascertained from information provided
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CV of Vitamin D is more than DBP

The coefficient of variation of vitamin D is more than that of diastolic blood pressure.

The coefficient of variation (CV) is given by the formula:

CV = 100(s/x̅)

where,

CV = Coefficient of variation

s = standard deviation

x̅ = mean

Substituting the data given in the question, in the above formula,

The CV of diastolic blood pressure is:

CV(DBP)= 100(11/110)

= 100(1/10)

= 10%

The CV of vitamin D is

CV(Vitamin D)= 100(3/18)

= 100(1/6)

= 16.67%

Therefore, the CV of vitamin D is more than the CV of DBP.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On administration of phenylephrine, the following change was noted as shown in the images below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nodular episcleritis

The image shows a nodule surrounded by redness. On administration of phenylephrine, blanching of superficial episcleral vessels is seen. Hence, the probable diagnosis is nodular episcleritis.

2.5% phenylephrine can be used to differentiate episcleritis and scleritis. Since the vessels of the episclera are superficial, they blanch. Whereas, in scleritis, the vessels do not blanch.

Episcleritis is benign, recurrent, inflammation of the episclera, involving the overlying Tenon's capsule but not the underlying sclera. It is more common in women than in men. It is an allergic reaction to an endogenous toxin. It is commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Episcleritis is characterized by redness, mild ocular discomfort described as a gritty, burning, or foreign body sensation

Clinically, two types of presentations may occur:

• Simple episcleritis is characterized by sectorial or diffuse inflammation of the episclera.
• Nodular episcleritis is characterized by a pink or purple flat nodule surrounded by injection, usually situated 2-3 mm away from the limbus. The nodule is firm, and tender and can be moved separately from the sclera, and the overlying conjunctiva also moves freely.

Treatment includes topical NSAIDs, corticosteroid eye drops, cold compress, and artificial tears. In recurrent cases, systemic NSAIDs are used.

Scleritis refers to an inflammation of the sclera proper. It usually occurs in elderly patients (40-70 years) involving females more than males. It is frequently associated with an underlying systemic inflammatory condition. The patient presents with moderate to severe pain, redness, lacrimation, photophobia, and diminution of vision.

Scleritis can be classified as immune-mediated non-infectious scleritis and infectious scleritis. Immune-mediated non-infectious scleritis is further classified as:

I. Anterior sclerltis (98%)

a. Non-necrotizing scleritis (85%)

• Diffuse
• Nodular

b. Necrotizing scleritis(13%)

1. With inflammation:

• Vasa-occlusive
• Granulomatous
• Surgically induced

2. Without inflammation(scleromalacia perforans).

II. Posterior scleritis (2%)

Treatment options include:

• Non-necrotizing scleritis- Topical steroids and systemic indomethacin.
• Necrotizing scleritis- Topical and oral steroids, immunosuppressive agents and surgical treatment like scleral patch graft.
• Infectious scleritis- Antimicrobial therapy, and surgical debridement.

Other options-

Option C: Tenon's cyst or conjunctival inclusion cyst is a benign condition filled with serous fluid and slimy mucous secretions of congenital or acquired origin. Acquired cysts can occur following strabismus surgery, pars plana vitrectomy, scleral buckling, and Ahmed glaucoma valve insertion. The patient presents with swelling near the limbus with no pain or redness. The consistency is cystic to firm, non-tender with no mobility suggesting that the cyst is adherent to the underlying scleral tissue.

Option D: Phlycten is a white-pinkish nodule surrounded by hyperemia on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction due to endogenous allergens like Staphylococcus aureus (most common) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Treatment includes topical steroids; atropine if the cornea is involved.
questions.learning: Nodular episcleritis — The image shows a nodule surrounded by redness. On administration of phenylephrine, blanching of superficial episcleral vessels is seen.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What MRI imaging technique is being depicted in the image provided among the options?
questions.explanation: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) uses different pulse sequences to highlight various tissues. In a "T2-weighted MRI," fluid, such as "Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)," appears characteristically "bright white". This sequence is excellent for identifying edema, inflammation, and demyelination, which also appear bright. In contrast, in a T1-weighted MRI (Option A), CSF appears dark (black), while white matter appears brighter than grey matter. FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery, Option D) is a T2-weighted sequence where the "fluid signal is suppressed" (turned black) to make periventricular lesions more visible. STIR (Short Tau Inversion Recovery, Option C) is a fat-suppressed sequence often used in musculoskeletal imaging. Identifying these basic sequences is fundamental for interpreting neuroimaging. T2 weighting is particularly useful for visualizing pathological processes since most diseased tissues have an increased water content, making them hyperintense (bright) relative to the surrounding healthy anatomy
questions.learning: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) uses different pulse sequences to highlight various tissues. In a "T2-weighted MRI," fluid, such as "Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)," appears characteristically "bright white".

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a situation where a woman married for four years dies and leaves a suicide note alleging dowry-related harassment, who is legally authorized to conduct the investigation?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC Section 176), a Magisterial Inquest is mandatory in specific suspicious circumstances. This includes cases where a woman dies within seven years of marriage, whether it is by suicide (as in this case with the note), homicide, or under any other suspicious circumstances related to dowry. The investigation must be conducted by an Executive or Judicial Magistrate rather than just the police. The Police (Option A) conduct a standard "Police Inquest" (Section 174) for most other unnatural deaths, but dowry-related deaths are protected by the requirement for higher-level judicial oversight. The Village headman (Option B) has no legal authority to conduct such investigations. A Judge (Option C) presides over trials but does not typically conduct initial death investigations (inquests). This law ensures that sensitive dowry-related deaths are scrutinized to prevent the covering up of "dowry deaths" as simple suicides. Thus, the Magistrate is the responsible official

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The most common triggering factor of the given condition is ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Infection

The given image shows characteristic target lesions of erythema multiforme. This most commonly occurs following a herpes simplex virus infection.

The common triggers are:

• Herpes simplex infection
• Mycoplasma infection
• Bacterial infections
• Fungal infections
• Vaccinations
• Malignancy- carcinoma, lymphoma, leukemia
• Drugs- sulfonamides, rifampicin, penicillins, hydantoin derivatives
• Miscellaneous- lupus erythematosus (Rowell Syndrome), sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa

Erythema multiforme is best regarded as a self‐limiting cytotoxic dermatitis resulting from cell‐mediated hypersensitivity.

It presents clinically with a spectrum of macular, papular, or urticarial lesions, as well as the classic acral iris or ‘target lesions’.

Target lesions are less than 3 cm in diameter, rounded, and have three zones:

1. Central area of dusky erythema or purpura
2. Middle paler zone of edema
3. Outer ring of erythema with a well‐defined edge

Lesions may involve the palms and the trunk. Oral and genital mucosal membranes lesions are associated with erosions

The image below shows target lesions.
questions.learning: Infection — The given image shows characteristic target lesions of erythema multiforme. This most commonly occurs following a herpes simplex virus infection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Dietary fibres have:
options: Sometimes anabolic and sometimes catabolic effect, depending on the type
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No metabolic effect

Dietary fiber (roughage) consists of non-digestible plant carbohydrates such as cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, lignin, gums, and mucilage. Since humans lack the enzymes to digest fiber, it does not provide energy or participate directly in anabolic or catabolic metabolism. Therefore, it has no direct metabolic effect.

• Dietary fiber has no direct metabolic effect because it is not digested or absorbed. ⭐
• Soluble fiber (pectin, gums, mucilage):

• Lowers serum cholesterol
• Slows glucose absorption
• Improves glycemic control

• Insoluble fiber (cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin):

• Increases stool bulk
• Prevents constipation
• Reduces colonic transit time
questions.learning: No metabolic effect Dietary fiber (roughage) consists of non-digestible plant carbohydrates such as cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, lignin, gums, and mucilage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: After an initial serum β-hCG test in a patient with suspected pregnancy, when should the repeat β-hCG level ideally be checked to assess viability or progression?
questions.explanation: In early pregnancy, the doubling time of serum β-hCG is a critical marker of trophoblastic health and pregnancy viability. The standard clinical practice is to repeat the test after 48 hours. In a viable intrauterine pregnancy, the β-hCG level is expected to rise by at least 66% over this 48-hour window. A slower rise or a plateau in levels is highly suspicious of an ectopic pregnancy, while falling levels typically indicate an ongoing miscarriage. Checking after 24 hours (Option A) is often too early to see a meaningful trend, while 72 or 96 hours (Options C and D) may delay a critical diagnosis if the patient is unstable. Additionally, the "discriminatory zone" (usually ≥1,500 IU/L) is used alongside these trends to confirm the presence of a gestational sac on ultrasound
questions.learning: In early pregnancy, the doubling time of serum β-hCG is a critical marker of trophoblastic health and pregnancy viability. The standard clinical practice is to repeat the test after 48 hours.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient developed hypotension, bradycardia and apnea on injection of an irritant substance. Which of the following physiological reflexes is involved in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bezold-jarisch reflex

The circulatory collapse, apnea in a patient following injection of irritant is due to Bezold-Jarisch Reflex.

It is the activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibres in the cardiopulmonary region (e.g. juxta capillary region of alveoli, ventricles, atria, great veins, and pulmonary artery) that causes profound bradycardia, hypotension and a brief period of apnea followed by rapid shallow breathing

It can be elicited by :

* Substances like capsaicin, serotonin, phenyl biguanide, veratridine

* Myocardial ischemia and reperfusion as a result of increased production of oxygen radicals

* Radiocontrast agents for coronary angiography

Other options:

Option A: Tachycardia following acute volume overload is due to the Bainbridge Reflex. The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain. Efferent signals are then transmitted back through vagal and sympathetic nerves to increase heart rate and strength of heart contraction.

Option B: Hypertension following a head injury is due to the Cushing Reflex. When the intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to RVLM neurons is compromised. The local hypoxia and hypercapnia cause an increase in discharge from the neurons, producing hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration. The resultant rise in systemic arterial pressure tends to restore the blood flow to the medulla.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child was brought to the OPD with a painless swelling near the outer canthus of the eye since childhood. The swelling is slow-growing, non-tender, and firm with normal overlying skin. On palpation, it is not compressible and appears to be fixed. There are no signs of inflammation, discharge, or change in size on straining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Angular dermoid cyst

An angular dermoid cyst is a congenital inclusion cyst that develops due to entrapment of ectodermal tissue along embryonic lines of fusion. It typically presents as a painless, slowly enlarging swelling near the lateral end of the eyebrow (superolateral orbital margin) in children.

Why not the other options?

• B. Lipoma: Soft, lobulated, freely mobile, usually occurs in adults.
• C. Sebaceous cyst: Has a punctum, arises from the skin, uncommon near the eyebrow in children.
• D. Epidermoid cyst: Usually occurs in adults and is more mobile; less commonly found at the lateral orbital rim.
questions.learning: Angular dermoid cyst — An angular dermoid cyst is a congenital inclusion cyst that develops due to entrapment of ectodermal tissue along embryonic lines of fusion.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with fever, cough, conjunctival congestion, and coryza. On examination, there are red maculopapular rashes on the neck and forehead. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Measles

The clinical features of cough, conjunctivitis and coryza along with fever with rash leads to a diagnosis of measles.

Measles is a common cause of fever with rash that spread via droplets. Apart from the characteristic prodrome. it presents with Koplik spots I.E white grain lesions with surrounding erythema on the buccal mucosa opposite to the lower second molar. The rash macular rash of measles begins behind the ears on the 4th day, rapidly becomes maculopapular and spreads to the face, neck, chest, arms, trunk, thighs and legs.

Other options:

Option A: Mumps is caused by a paramyxovirus and spread by droplets and contact. It causes fever, malaise unilateral or bilateral parotitis. It also causes epididymo-orchitis in males.

Option C: Chickenpox is caused by varicella zoster and spreads by contact and airborne. It has a prodrome of fever, malaise, anorexia and headache which is followed by a rash in 1-2 days. It has pruritic erythematous macules that first appear on the trunk and spreads to face and extremities that evolve into papules, vesicles and pustules that become crusted. The presence of several crops of lesions that are in different stages of evolution is a characteristic of varicella.

Option D: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is caused by parvovirus B19 transmitted by airborne route. The prodromal consists of low-grade fever, headache and mild upper respiratory tract infection. An erythematous slapped cheeked rash that first appears on the face is characteristic. A macular rash then spreads to the trunk and extremities that undergoes central clearing giving a lacy or reticulated pattern.

Pearl PF0095: Viral infections associated with rash

Viral infection
Rash characteristics

Chickenpox
Appears 1st day of fever, centripetal, pleomorphic, dewdrops on rose petal appearance

Measles
Appears on the 4th day over the face and retroauricular origin

Rubella
Rash on day 1 over the face

Erythema infectiosum

Rash on cheeks (slapped cheek appearance), moves to trunk and extremities

Exanthem subitum
Macules or maculopapular rash

Infectious mononucleosis
Associated with maculopapular rash
questions.learning: Measles — The clinical features of cough, conjunctivitis and coryza along with fever with rash leads to a diagnosis of measles. Measles is a common cause of fever with rash that spread via droplets.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: eFAST is least helpful in diagnosing which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retroperitoneal hematoma

Among the given options, eFAST (focussed assessment with sonography in trauma) is the least useful in diagnosing retroperitoneal hematoma as the sensitivity of ultrasound for the detection of retroperitoneal hematomas is extremely poor.

Computed Tomography (CT Scan) is the investigation of choice for retroperitoneal injury, but it can only be done in a hemodynamically stable patient.

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography used to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries.

Technique:

• The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:

• Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
• Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
• Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
• Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

1. Operator-dependent
2. Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.
3. Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries
4. Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum
5. Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma
6. May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: If DNA is damaged in the cell cycle, which gene causes cell cycle arrest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. p53

If the DNA is damaged in the cell cycle, the p53 gene causes arrest of the cell cycle in G1 phase to provide time for DNA repair. In case the DNA damage could not be repaired, p53 triggers apoptosis.

In conditions where there is mutation in p53 gene, the cells with damaged DNA continue to replicate and thus may undergo neoplastic transformation.
questions.learning: p53 If the DNA is damaged in the cell cycle, the p53 gene causes arrest of the cell cycle in G1 phase to provide time for DNA repair. In case the DNA damage could not be repaired, p53 triggers apoptosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Management of an appendicular mass in appendicitis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ochsner–Sherren regimen

Ochsner–Sherren regimen is indicated for patients with appendicular mass in whom conditions are stable.

The patient's temperature and pulse rate are recorded 4-hourly and adequate fluid balance is maintained. CECT abdomen is done and antibiotic therapy is started. Abscess if present is drained. Improvement is usually seen within 24–48 hours.

Ochsner–Sherren regimen:

Principle :

* The inflammatory process is already localised and that inadvertent surgery is difficult and may be dangerous.

* It may be impossible to find the appendix and, occasionally, a faecal fistula may form.

* Antibiotic therapy should be given after performing CECT abdomen

* Abscess if present can be drained radiologically.

Outcome :

* Improvement in 24–48 h

* 90% cases resolve

* Failure should raise suspicion of Crohn’s disease and carcinoma.

Criteria for stopping conservative treatment of Appendicular mass:

* Rising pulse rate

* Increasing or spreading abdominal pain

* Increasing size of the mass

Other options:

* Alvarado score is a clinical scoring system used in the diagnosis of appendicitis.

* If the patient's condition deteriorates or if there is evidence of peritonitis, laparotomy is performed.

* Incision and drainage are not done in appendicitis.
questions.learning: Ochsner–Sherren regimen Ochsner–Sherren regimen is indicated for patients with appendicular mass in whom conditions are stable. The patient's temperature and pulse rate are recorded 4-hourly and adequate fluid balance is maintained.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with lower abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Stool examination reveals the findings shown below. Which organism is the most likely cause of this infection?
questions.explanation: The image displays an Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite, characterized by its distinctive central nucleus and potentially ingested red blood cells. This parasite is the causative agent of amoebic dysentery, which classically presents with lower abdominal pain, diarrhea, and bloody stools. Trophozoites cause significant tissue destruction in the colon, leading to characteristic "flask-shaped" ulcerations. Giardia lamblia (Option A) presents with non-bloody, greasy stools and has a "pear-shaped" trophozoite with two nuclei. Shigella dysenteriae (Option B) and Campylobacter jejuni (Option D) are bacterial causes of dysentery; while they present with similar symptoms, they would not show these characteristic large protozoal trophozoites on microscopic stool examination. Therefore, based on the specific protozoal morphology shown, Entamoeba histolytica is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The afferent limb of the corneal (wisp) reflex is carried by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), specifically via the nasociliary nerve.
questions.explanation: The corneal reflex (blink reflex) is a protective mechanism that triggers bilateral eyelid closure when the cornea is stimulated. The Trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically the ophthalmic division (V1), is responsible for the afferent limb of this reflex. Sensory fibers from the cornea travel via the nasociliary branch of V1 to the trigeminal sensory nucleus in the brainstem. The Facial nerve (CN VII) (Option A) mediates the efferent limb, sending motor signals to the orbicularis oculi muscle to contract and close the eye. The Oculomotor nerve (CN III) (Option C) controls eyelid elevation and most extraocular muscles but is not part of this reflex pathway. The Abducens nerve (CN VI) (Option D) is responsible for lateral eye movement and is unrelated to the blink response. Clinically, testing this reflex is essential for assessing brainstem integrity and the function of cranial nerves V and VII
questions.learning: The corneal reflex (blink reflex) is a protective mechanism that triggers bilateral eyelid closure when the cornea is stimulated. The Trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically the ophthalmic division (V1), is responsible for the afferent limb of this reflex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on chlorthalidone. At his follow-up visit, his blood glucose levels are found to be significantly elevated despite adherence to antidiabetic therapy. Which of the following best explains the mechanism responsible for this adverse effect?
options: Chlorthalidone causes hypokalemia, which reduces insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells
Chlorthalidone directly stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis by activating glucagon receptors
Chlorthalidone increases insulin secretion, leading to receptor downregulation and hyperglycemia
Chlorthalidone inhibits GLUT-4 translocation in skeletal muscle, causing insulin resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlorthalidone causes hypokalemia, which reduces insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells

Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (e.g., chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide) can cause hyperglycemia by inducing hypokalemia, which impairs insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells. Potassium is essential for normal β-cell depolarization and insulin release; therefore, hypokalemia decreases insulin secretion, leading to worsening glycemic control, particularly in patients with diabetes mellitus.

Why not the other options?

• B. Chlorthalidone directly stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis by activating glucagon receptors: Thiazides do not activate glucagon receptors.
• C. Chlorthalidone increases insulin secretion, leading to receptor downregulation and hyperglycemia: Incorrect; thiazides decrease, rather than increase, insulin secretion.
• D. Chlorthalidone inhibits GLUT-4 translocation in skeletal muscle, causing insulin resistance: This is not the primary mechanism of thiazide-induced hyperglycemia.
questions.learning: Chlorthalidone causes hypokalemia, which reduces insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (e.g., chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide) can cause hyperglycemia by inducing hypokalemia, which impairs insulin secretion…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Fundoscopy findings are shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CRAO

The given fundus picture showing a cherry-red spot is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO):

Risk factors include:

* Heart disease

* Carotid artery disease

* Mucormycosis

* Varicella infection

* Radiation exposure

* Trauma

Etiology:

* Emboli - emboli having carotid artery or cardiac origin are the most common cause of CRAO. Other emboli are - cholesterol emboli, calcium emboli, and platelet fibrin emboli

* Atherosclerosis-related thrombosis

* Retinal arteritis with obliteration

* Angiospasm

* Raised intraocular pressure

* Thrombophilic disorders

Clinical features are:

* Sudden painless loss of vision

* Amaurosis fugax - transient monocular blindness that is due to ischemia. As seen in this patient.

* Direct pupillary reflex is absent

* Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is positive

Fundus examination shows:

* Marked attenuation of arteries – thread like arteries

* Interrupted blood flow in vein – cattle track appearance

* Cherry red spot

* Severe edema

* Retinal pallor

Treatment is to dislodge the emboli by suddenly decreasing the IOP by I/V acetazolamide or ocular massage. Ocular massage is considered the most effective method. Other treatment options include IV mannitol, vasodilators (nitrates), fibrinolytic therapy, or laser photo disruption in some cases. In cases of giant cell arteritis, steroids are beneficial.

Other options:

Option B: In CRVO, funduscopy shows engorged and tortuous retinal veins, massive retinal hemorrhages with splashed tomato appearance, and cotton wool spots.

Option C: Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy can have microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhage, and mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA). Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is characterized by neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) or neovascularization elsewhere (NVE).

Option D: In cystoid macular edema, the fundus shows a dull foveal reflex/absent foveal reflex. The fluorescein angiography image shows a flower petal pattern.

Pearl PF1384: Important causes of cherry-red spots

* Commotio retinae

* Central retinal and cilioretinal artery occlusion

* Metabolic storage diseases

* GM1 gangliosidosis

* Mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis)

* GM2 gangliosidosis (Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff disease)

* Farber disease

* Niemann–Pick disease

* Retinotoxicity due to specific agents, including quinine, dapsone, gentamicin, carbon monoxide, and methanol
questions.learning: CRAO — The given fundus picture showing a cherry-red spot is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO): Risk factors include: * Heart disease * Carotid artery disease * Mucormycosis * Varicella infection…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who was a known case of rheumatoid arthritis is brought to the ER due to dizziness. Her BP was 90/60mmHg. She was prescribed a medication by her local doctor which she stopped taking suddenly. Her blood sugar was low and serum potassium was 6mEq/L. Which of the following drugs should be given to her next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrocortisone

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life-threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones. If a patient displays features of adrenal insufficiency, treatment must immediately be commenced, before awaiting the biochemical diagnosis. Intravenous administration of hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours, >2 litres of saline is given in 6 hours under careful cardiovascular monitoring.

The symptoms of adrenal insufficiency are as follows:

• Glucocorticoid deficiency leads to:

• Fatigue, lack of energy
• Weight loss, anorexia
• Myalgia
• Hypoglycemia
• Low blood pressure, postural hypotension

• Mineralocorticoid deficiency leads to:

• Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting
• Dizziness, postural hypotension
• Low blood pressure, postural hypotension
• Hyponatremia
• Hyperkalemia

• Adrenal androgen deficiency leads to dry and itchy skin, loss of libido
• The hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas results from excess ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) secretion which occurs in response to decreased adrenal cortical hormones.

Primary causes of the Addisonian crisis include:

• Adrenal haemorrhage
• Acute infection

Secondary causes of the Addisonian crisis include:

• Surgery
• Cessation of steroid therapy
• Postpartum pituitary necrosis.
questions.learning: Hydrocortisone — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life-threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mIU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single dose methotrexate

A patient on infertility treatment, with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding with beta hCG levels of 2800 mIU/mL, and a gestational sac in the left adnexa points to the diagnosis of unruptured ectopic pregnancy and the most appropriate management is single-dose methotrexate.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without intervention and can be managed expectantly.

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

• Hemodynamic stability
• Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL
• Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.
• Patients are willing and able to comply with post-treatment follow-up and have access to emergency medical services within a reasonable time frame in case of a deterioration in the clinical status.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

• Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met
• Gestational sac >3.5 cm
• Fetal cardiac activity present
• Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL
• Significant pain and hemoperitoneum
• Failure of expectant or medical management
• Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention
• Doubtful compliance with medical management

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy.
