questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which type of thyroid carcinoma is most commonly associated with prior radiation exposure and is characterized by frequent RET/ PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations?
questions.explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common form of thyroid cancer and is strongly associated with a history of ionizing radiation exposure, particularly during childhood. Molecularly, it is characterized by RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations, which drive the tumorigenesis. Follicular carcinoma (Option A) is more often linked to iodine deficiency and typically shows RAS mutations or PAX8-PPAR$\gamma$ translocations. Anaplastic carcinoma (Option C) is a highly aggressive, undifferentiated tumor that often arises in long-standing goiters and has a very poor prognosis. Medullary carcinoma (Option D) arises from the C-cells and is uniquely associated with germline RET mutations in MEN 2 syndromes, but it is not classically linked to radiation exposure like the papillary type. Papillary carcinoma is distinguished histologically by "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei and Psammoma bodies. Due to its well-defined link to radiation and specific genetic markers, papillary carcinoma is the definitive answer. Early diagnosis usually leads to an excellent survival rate
questions.learning: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common form of thyroid cancer and is strongly associated with a history of ionizing radiation exposure, particularly during childhood.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: New A 33-year-old male comes with complaints of dry cough, fever, and shortness of breath for 2 days along with a loss of taste and smell. He is a social worker who has been traveling a lot. What would be the investigation of choice for this patient to confirm the diagnosis of COVID-19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RT-PCR

The patient with the above clinical scenario is most likely suffering from COVID-19. RT-PCR (reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction) is the investigation of choice to confirm an acute infection of COVID-19.

There are two major types of tests for COVID-19:

* Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs; eg, RT-PCR) –
RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 is the primary test used to diagnose active COVID-19. The test is typically performed on nasopharyngeal swabs, but can also be performed on other respiratory tract specimens (eg, oropharyngeal swabs, lower respiratory tract samples).

* Serology –
Serologic tests measure antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 and are primarily used to identify patients who have had COVID-19 in the past. While some serologic assays can help identify patients with acute infection, they are not as reliable as RT-PCR and not recommended for this purpose.

Basic protective measures against the new coronavirus: (SARS CoV 2)

* Wash your hands frequently for at least 20 seconds.

* Maintain social distancing- Maintain at least 1-meter distance between yourself and anyone who is coughing or sneezing

* Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth

* Practice respiratory hygiene- cover your mouth and nose with your bent elbow or tissue when you cough or sneeze, then dispose of the used tissue immediately.

* If you have fever, cough, and difficulty breathing, seek medical care early

* Stay informed and follow the advice given by your healthcare provider

Treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment recommended for COVID-19. People with COVID-19 should receive supportive care to help relieve symptoms. For severe cases, treatment should include care to support vital organ functions.
questions.learning: RT-PCR — The patient with the above clinical scenario is most likely suffering from COVID-19. RT-PCR (reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction) is the investigation of choice to confirm an acute infection of COVID-19.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The recommended approach for managing an angular dermoid cyst is:
questions.explanation: An angular dermoid cyst is a congenital developmental cyst, most commonly found at the lateral end of the eyebrow (external angular dermoid). These cysts contain keratin, hair follicles, and sebaceous material. The standard and most effective management is complete surgical excision (Option A). This is typically performed for aesthetic reasons and to prevent complications such as secondary infection or progressive bony erosion. Radiotherapy (Option B) is strictly used for malignancies and has no role in benign dermoid cysts. Antibiotics (Option C) are only indicated if the cyst becomes acutely infected (abscess), but they will not remove the cyst itself. Intralesional steroids (Option D) are used for inflammatory conditions like chalazia or hemangiomas, not for sebum-filled dermoid cysts. Therefore, surgical removal remains the definitive curative approach. Clinicians must ensure the entire cyst wall is removed to prevent recurrence. This procedure is generally considered low-risk and highly effective
questions.learning: An angular dermoid cyst is a congenital developmental cyst, most commonly found at the lateral end of the eyebrow (external angular dermoid). These cysts contain keratin, hair follicles, and sebaceous material.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a swollen foot and multiple sinuses as shown in the below image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mycetoma

The most likely diagnosis here is Mycetoma which is caused by Eumycetoma.

Mycetoma:-

• Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, fascia and bone, which most often affects the foot or the hand. It is, therefore, commonly known as Maduramycosis or Madura foot. Mycetoma occurs worldwide.
• Etiology:  It can be divided into three types, eumycetomas, actinomycetomas and botryomycosis.

Pathogenesis:-

• Triad of symptoms: Infection follows traumatic inoculation of the organism into the subcutaneous tissue from soil or vegetable sources, usually on thorns or splinters and results in tumefactions, deformities and draining sinuses discharging fungal colonies called grains or granules (triad of symptoms).
• Subcutaneous tissues of the feet, lower extremities, hands, and exposed areas are most often involved.
• Grains: Within host tissues the organisms develop to form compacted colonies (grains) 0.5–2 mm in diameter, the color of which depends on the organism responsible.

Laboratory Diagnosis

• A. Direct Examination: The presence of grains in pus collected from draining sinuses or in biopsy material is diagnostic.
• B. Culture Samples should also be cultured, at both 25–30°C and 37°C, on brain-heart infusion agar or blood agar for actinomycetes and on Sabouraud agar (without cycloheximide) for fungi.

Treatment:-

The management of eumycetoma is difficult, involving surgical debridement or excision and chemotherapy. Actinomycetoma responds well to rifampicin in combination with sulfonamides or cotrimoxazole.
questions.learning: Mycetoma — The most likely diagnosis here is Mycetoma which is caused by Eumycetoma. Mycetoma:- • Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, fascia and bone, which most often affects the foot or the hand.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young girl presents with continuous urinary dribbling despite normal voiding and has never achieved full continence since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of continuous dribbling of urine in a female patient who otherwise voids normally is the pathognomonic presentation of an Ectopic Ureter (Option A). In these cases (often associated with a duplex system), the ureter bypasses the urinary sphincter and opens into the vagina or vestibule. Because the opening is distal to the sphincter, urine leaks out continuously. However, because the other ureter is normally positioned in the bladder, the child can still void normally. Ureterocele (Option B), congenital megaureter (Option C), and Vesicoureteric reflux (Option D) are all internal urinary abnormalities that may cause infections or obstruction but do not cause this specific "leakage while voiding" paradox. Therefore, because the symptoms date back to birth and follow this unique pattern, ectopic ureter is the definitive diagnosis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by intravenous urography or MRI. Surgical reimplantation into the bladder is the curative treatment
questions.learning: The clinical history of continuous dribbling of urine in a female patient who otherwise voids normally is the pathognomonic presentation of an Ectopic Ureter (Option A).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A full-term male newborn is noted to have the following appearance. Which of the following best describes the associated abnormalities in this congenital condition?
options: Urinary tract anomalies with undescended testes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urinary tract anomalies with undescended testes

Prune Belly syndrome (Eagle–Barrett syndrome) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by the classic triad of:

1. Partial or complete absence of the anterior abdominal wall muscles → wrinkled, "prune-like" abdomen
2. Urinary tract anomalies → dilated ureters, megacystis, hydronephrosis, posterior urethral obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux
3. Bilateral cryptorchidism (undescended testes)

It occurs almost exclusively in male infants. Urinary tract abnormalities may lead to recurrent urinary tract infections, renal dysplasia, and chronic kidney disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. Acute subpubic angle: Incorrect. This is a pelvic anatomical feature and is not a characteristic finding of Prune Belly syndrome.
• C. Bilateral undescended ovaries: Incorrect. Ovaries do not descend into the inguinal canal like testes. The syndrome is classically associated with bilateral cryptorchidism in males.
• D. Tracheoesophageal fistula: Incorrect. This is a separate congenital anomaly, commonly associated with esophageal atresia, and is unrelated to Prune Belly syndrome.
questions.learning: Urinary tract anomalies with undescended testes Prune Belly syndrome (Eagle–Barrett syndrome) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by the classic triad of: 1.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Methyl-tetrahydro-folic acid gets accumulated in deficiency of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B12

Accumulation of methyl tetrahydro folic acid is seen in vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 acts as a cofactor of methionine synthase, an enzyme involved in the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate from methyl-tetrahydrofolate. Hence, in vitamin B12 deficiency methyl-tetrahydrofolate accumulates leading to functional folate deficiency known as the folate trap.

The conversion of 5,10-methylene-THF into 5-methyl-THF (methyltetrahydrofolate) is an irreversible process. The major source of tetrahydrofolate for tissues is 5-methyl-THF. The only way to make further use of 5-methyl-THF and to maintain the folate cycle is by the vitamin B12-dependent remethylation of homocysteine to methionine by the methionine synthase enzyme.

Decreased activity of methionine synthase in vitamin B12 deficiency results in the accumulation of methyltetrahydrofolate, which cannot be used, resulting in a folate trap. The folate cycle acts as the link between the functions of folate and vitamin B12, and deficiency of vitamin B12 can cause a functional deficiency of folate.

Note: Since vitamin B12 is also linked to the regeneration of methionine from homocysteine, its deficiency can result in hyperhomocysteinemia as well. This in turn increases the risk of atherosclerosis, hypertension, and thrombosis.
questions.learning: B12 Accumulation of methyl tetrahydro folic acid is seen in vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 acts as a cofactor of methionine synthase, an enzyme involved in the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate from methyl-tetrahydrofolate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about polycythemia vera is true?
options: Risk of thrombosis strongly correlates with the degree of thrombocytosis
Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation
It is protective against H.pylori infection
Acute myeloid leukemia is the most common cause of mortality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation

Generalized pruritus seen in polycythemia vera (PV) is a consequence of the activation of mast cells by JAK 2 mutation.

Other options:

Option A: The risk of thrombosis strongly correlates with erythrocytosis, not the degree of thrombocytosis.

Option C: In polycythemia vera, there is an increased risk of H.pylori infection.

Option D: Thrombosis is the major cause of mortality in polycythemia vera. The incidence of acute leukemia in patients not exposed to chemotherapy or radiation therapy is low.

PV is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder in which red cells, granulocytes & platelets accumulate in the absence of a physiological stimulus. The most common mutation seen in PV is the JAK2 mutation.

Clinical features of polycythemia vera are:

• Thrombosis is the most common manifestation and is the major cause of mortality. Uncontrolled erythrocytosis causes increased viscosity of the blood causing thrombosis of the vessels. Patients may present with stroke, transient ischemic attacks, myocardial infarction, and Budd-Chiari syndrome.
• Aquagenic pruritis is generalized itching following a warm bath or a shower due to increased mast cells and histamine.
• Erythromelalgia is erythema and pain in the fingers, hands, and feet due to increased platelet stickiness.
• Splenomegaly due to increased destruction of RBCs in the spleen
• Gout is due to the excessive proliferation of the marrow cells leading to elevated uric acid levels.
questions.learning: Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation Generalized pruritus seen in polycythemia vera (PV) is a consequence of the activation of mast cells by JAK 2 mutation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which substance is involved in the conjugation process in the liver?
questions.explanation: The liver performs conjugation to make various endogenous and exogenous substances more water-soluble for easier excretion. The most significant substance involved in this Phase II metabolic process is glucuronic acid. Through the action of the enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT), glucuronic acid is attached to molecules like bilirubin, steroid hormones, and many drugs. Hyaluronic acid (Option A) is a major component of the extracellular matrix in connective tissues. Gluconic acid (Option B) and glycolic acid (Option D) are organic acids that are not the primary agents used for hepatic conjugation. Efficient glucuronidation is vital for detoxifying the body; for example, the conjugation of bilirubin is essential to prevent kernicterus in newborns and chronic jaundice in adults. This biochemical pathway is a cornerstone of clinical pharmacology and toxicology, as many drug-drug interactions occur because different medications compete for the same glucuronidation pathways in the liver
questions.learning: The liver performs conjugation to make various endogenous and exogenous substances more water-soluble for easier excretion. The most significant substance involved in this Phase II metabolic process is glucuronic acid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient underwent gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. Which of the following vitamins needs to be supplemented in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12

A patient who has undergone gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma needs to be supplemented with vitamin B12.

Vitamin B12 absorption is a complex process that relies on several factors. Intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach, is essential for this process. Gastric acid and pepsin release vitamin B12 from dietary proteins, allowing it to bind with cobalophilin in the saliva. In the jejunum, cobalophilin is broken down, freeing vitamin B12 to bind with intrinsic factor. This complex is then absorbed in the distal ileum through specific receptors.  Following gastrectomy, the production of intrinsic factor is impaired due to the removal of gastric tissue, making vitamin B12 absorption difficult. Therefore, vitamin B12 supplementation is necessary after gastrectomy to prevent deficiency.

Other complications of gastrectomy include:

• Nutritional deficiencies- Iron deficiency anemia (most common), Vitamin B12 deficiency, and osteoporosis
• Dumping syndrome: early and late
• Diarrhea
• Duodenal stump leak/blow out
• Bile reflux gastritis and esophagitis
• Gall stones
• Roux syndrome
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 — A patient who has undergone gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma needs to be supplemented with vitamin B12. Vitamin B12 absorption is a complex process that relies on several factors.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presented with pain in the hand. The joints involved were proximal interphalangeal joint, distal interphalangeal joint and first carpometacarpal joint. The wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints were spared. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Osteoarthritis

The most likely diagnosis is osteoarthritis (OA) of the hand.

In OA of the hand, the joints involved are the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints (DIP & PIP), and the first carpometacarpal joint (base of the thumb), while the metacarpophalangeal (MCP)  joint, wrist, elbow, and ankle are usually spared.

The nodules palpable in the DIP are called Heberden’s nodes, while those palpable in the PIP are called Bouchard’s nodes.

The image below shows OA of the hand:

Other options:

Option B: There is relative sparing of the DIP joint in rheumatoid arthritis.

Option C: Psoriatic arthritis of the hands commonly involves the PIP, DIP, and metacarpophalangeal joints.

Option D: In pseudogout, the knee joint is most commonly affected, followed by the wrist, while the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is rarely affected.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Into which dural venous sinus does the great cerebral vein (vein of Galen) drain?
questions.explanation: The great cerebral vein (vein of Galen) is a short midline vein formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins. It drains blood from deep structures of the brain such as the thalamus, basal ganglia, and internal capsule. After formation, it passes posteriorly beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum. The vein of Galen empties into the straight sinus, which is located at the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. In the given diagram, label B corresponds to the straight sinus, making it the correct answer. The straight sinus also receives blood from the inferior sagittal sinus and sometimes the occipital sinus. From here, blood flows into the confluence of sinuses, and then into transverse and sigmoid sinuses before reaching the internal jugular vein. Why other options are incorrect: (A) (Superior sagittal sinus) → drains superficial veins (C) (Transverse sinus) → downstream channel (D) (Sigmoid sinus) → final drainage pathway
questions.learning: The great cerebral vein (vein of Galen) is a short midline vein formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins. It drains blood from deep structures of the brain such as the thalamus, basal ganglia, and internal capsule.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A mother noticed a mucopurulent discharge from the right puncta of her 3-month-old child. There is a history of increased watering in his right eye. Which of the following is the appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sac massage with topical antibiotics

The above history of epiphora (increased watering) and mucopurulent discharge from the punctum is suggestive of congenital dacryocystitis.

Congenital dacrocystitis is the chronic inflammation of the lacrimal sac. It occurs due to the stasis of secretions which in turn is due to congenital blockage of the nasolacrimal duct.

Regurgitation test (applying pressure over the lacrimal sac causes regurgitation of mucopurulent discharge from the lower punctum) is usually positive.

More than 90% of patients with congenital nasolacrimal obstruction undergo spontaneous resolution by 1 year of age.

Treatment depends on the age of the child:

* Less than 9 months

* Massaging (Crigler’s massage, which increases the hydrostatic pressure)

* Antibiotics eye drops

* 9 months to 4 years

* Probing

* Older children (> 4 years):

* Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)

* In DCR, an opening is made into the nasal cavity from the lacrimal sac.

* DCR gives the best result.
questions.learning: Sac massage with topical antibiotics — The above history of epiphora (increased watering) and mucopurulent discharge from the punctum is suggestive of congenital dacryocystitis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which among the following is not included in the severe acute malnutrition definition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Height for age

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is defined using indicators of acute nutritional status, not chronic growth failure.

Diagnostic criteria for SAM:

• Weight-for-height/length < −3 SD
• Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) < 11.5 cm (6–59 months)
• Presence of bilateral pitting edema

Why height-for-age is not included:

• Height-for-age reflects chronic malnutrition (stunting), not acute malnutrition
• SAM focuses on wasting and edema, which indicate recent or severe nutritional deficiency
questions.learning: Height for age Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is defined using indicators of acute nutritional status, not chronic growth failure. Diagnostic criteria for SAM: • Weight-for-height/length < −3 SD • Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) < 11.5 cm (6–59 months)…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following topical antifungal has both anti-inflammatory effects and anti-pruritic action?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sertaconazole

Sertaconazole has both anti-inflammatory effects and anti-pruritic action.

Sertaconazole inhibits the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from activated immune cells.
questions.learning: Sertaconazole Sertaconazole has both anti-inflammatory effects and anti-pruritic action. Sertaconazole inhibits the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from activated immune cells.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the structure marked in the CT scan ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cribriform plate

The structure marked in the image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The image shown is a coronal section of paranasal sinuses at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

The cribriform plate is identified as a bony structure that separates the nasal cavity from the anterior cranial fossa. It is part of the ethmoid bone and is a sieve-like structure as it is pierced by the olfactory nerve fibers.

Crista Galli is also a part of ethmoid bone that projects superiorly from the cribriform plate. It provides attachment for the falx cerebri.

The anterior ethmoidal canal is identified by its location below the roof of ethmoidal air cells. The anterior ethmoidal artery passes through this canal and it is important to identify this to avoid bleeding from this vessel during sinus surgeries.

The posterior ethmoid canal/foramen is an opening in the ethmoid bone through which the posterior ethmoidal artery, vein, and nerve traverse. It is not visualized in this image as it is a coronal section at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

The optic nerve can be identified as an oval intraorbital structure in the coronal sections.
questions.learning: Cribriform plate — The structure marked in the image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The image shown is a coronal section of paranasal sinuses at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 11-14 weeks

The best time to determine chorionicity and amnionicity in twin pregnancy is during the first trimester, especially between 11–14 weeks of gestation.

Why this period is ideal:

• Membranes and placental relationships are clearly visible
• Lambda (twin peak) sign and T-sign can be identified accurately
• Early diagnosis guides antenatal surveillance and management

Ultrasound findings:

• Lambda (twin peak) sign → dichorionic twins
• T-sign → monochorionic twins

Importance of determining chorionicity:

• Monochorionic twins have higher risks of:

• Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)
• Selective fetal growth restriction
• Twin anemia-polycythemia sequence
• Increased perinatal morbidity and mortality

Accuracy of chorionicity assessment decreases later in pregnancy as membranes become thinner and placentas may fuse.
questions.learning: 11-14 weeks The best time to determine chorionicity and amnionicity in twin pregnancy is during the first trimester, especially between 11–14 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure that the marked structure in the given image of atlas vertebra articulates with.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Occipital

The marked structure is the superior articular facet of the atlas (C1).

Atlas had large vertebral foramen, kidney-shaped superior articular facets, concave, and articulates with the occipital condyles to form the atlanto-occipital joint.

This joint permit flexion–extension movements of the head (“yes” nodding movement).
questions.learning: Occipital — The marked structure is the superior articular facet of the atlas (C1). Atlas had large vertebral foramen, kidney-shaped superior articular facets, concave, and articulates with the occipital condyles to form the atlanto-occipital joint.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The below phenomenon is due to
options: Case of suspension/hanging more than 72 hours
Case of immersion in water for 36 hours
Case of colliquative liquefaction due to immersion in hot water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Case of immersion in water for 36 hours

The given image shows maceration of the skin of the soles suggestive of washerwoman's feet/ washerwoman's skin. It is seen in a case of immersion in water for 36 hours.

Washerwoman's skin occurs if the body of the person has been immersed in water for a few hours to 3 days. The first signs tend to be on areas with an appreciable keratin layer (such as the fingertips, palms, backs of the hands, and later the soles) where the surface becomes wrinkled, pale, and sodden. This is called washerwoman’s skin. The first site affected is the fingerpads. It affects the hands earlier than the feet.

When a body falls into water in average temperate climates, the following is an approximate guide to timing:

Finding
Time since immersion

No wrinkling of finger pads
Less than a few hours

Wrinkled fingers, palms, and feet
Few hours to 3 days

Early decomposition (Head and abdomen)
4-10 days

The marbling of veins, peeling of the epidermis
2-4 weeks

Muscle loss with bone exposure
1-2 months

The other signs of immersion are:

1. Cutis anserina - goose-flesh or piloerection: This is usually found when the body is immersed in cold water.
2. Post-mortem hypostasis - If the water is still, the postmortem hypostasis affects the heads and the limbs. This is because the chest and abdomen float higher because of the lungs and the abdominal gases.
3. Foreign bodies in respiratory passages and stomach - Sand may be found deep in the respiratory passages and stomach, especially if the body has been rolled by the waves on a beach. This is not evidence of live aspiration.

Note: Signs of immersion just indicate that the body was immersed in water, they are not evidence of death from drowning.

Falanga (Option-A) also known as Falaka or Bastinado, is a method of torture that involves repeatedly striking the soles of the feet with an object such as a truncheon, iron rod, cable, bamboo cane, wooden pole, or rifle butt.

Glove-stocking-like staining (Option-B) is used to describe the purple-colored postmortem staining visualized in the dependent parts of the upper and lower limbs of a hanging victim. It is absent in postmortem hanging, where the pattern of hypostasis does not correspond with the position of suspension of the body

Liquefaction or colliquative changes begins by 5 days after death and becomes prominent in 10 days. Soft tissues change into semisolid masses which are black in color and get separated from bones and fall off.
questions.learning: Case of immersion in water for 36 hours — The given image shows maceration of the skin of the soles suggestive of washerwoman's feet/ washerwoman's skin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following are true about subclinical myocarditis? 1. Palpitations 2. Elevated BNP 3. Regional wall motion abnormalities in ECHO 4. Elevated troponin 5. Low LVEF in ECHO
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3, 4, 5

Subclinical myocarditis often lacks prominent symptoms but shows objective evidence of myocardial injury or dysfunction. Patients may have elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin), raised BNP due to myocardial stress, regional wall-motion abnormalities, and even reduced LVEF on echocardiography despite minimal symptoms.

1. Palpitations – Not a usual feature of myocarditis; thik of arrythmias when palpitations mentioned.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: What is the correct sequence of cellular events of inflammation? 1. Selectin 2. ICAM-1 3. CD31 4. IL-8
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

The cellular events of leukocyte recruitment in inflammation occur in a specific sequence:

1. Selectins → Mediate rolling of leukocytes along the endothelium.

2. ICAM-1 (Intercellular Adhesion Molecule-1) → Interacts with integrins to cause firm adhesion of leukocytes to the endothelium.

3. CD31 (PECAM-1) → Facilitates diapedesis/transmigration of leukocytes through the endothelial junctions.

4.  IL-8 (chemokine) → Directs chemotaxis, guiding leukocytes to the site of tissue injury.

Correct order: Selectin → ICAM-1 → CD31 → IL-8
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4 The cellular events of leukocyte recruitment in inflammation occur in a specific sequence: 1. Selectins → Mediate rolling of leukocytes along the endothelium.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: By which mechanism does gene repair occur when mediated by CRISPR-Cas9?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-homologous end joining

Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the major mechanism used by CRISPR-Cas9 for gene repair.

The CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) are clustered palindromic sequences found in many bacteria. It is a form of acquired immunity to infection by bacteriophages which complements the system of restriction endonucleases and methylases. CRISPR uses RNA-based targeting to bring the Cas9 endonuclease to foreign (or any complementary) DNA. Within bacteria this CRISPR-RNA-Cas9 complex then degrades and inactivates the targeted DNA.

The CRISPR system has been adapted for use in eukaryotic cells for gene deletion, gene editing and even modulation of gene transcription.
questions.learning: Non-homologous end joining Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the major mechanism used by CRISPR-Cas9 for gene repair. The CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) are clustered palindromic sequences found in many bacteria.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle aged woman presents with complaints of hearing her own voice and breath sounds. On examination, the tympanic membrane was moving with respiration. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rapid weight loss

The given clinical scenario where the patient hears her own voice and breath sounds is called autophony which is seen patulous eustachian tube.

Patulous eustachian tube is usually idiopathic where the tube is abnormally patent. But it is also seen in rapid weight loss, pregnancy especially the third trimester and patients with multiple sclerosis.

The eustachian tube valve is patulous and hence always open.This leads to the transfer of pressure changes in the nasal cavity to the middle ear and consequent movement of the tympanic membrane with respiration. This patent communication is the reason for hearing of own voice and breathing sounds

Treatment includes weight gain and administration of potassium iodide solution. In long-standing cases, specific treatment could include the cauterization of tubes or the insertion of the grommet.

Mass lesions of the nasal cavity may occlude the eustachian tube and cause fullness of the ear or otitis media, but won't cause any movement of tympanic membrane with respiration
questions.learning: Rapid weight loss — The given clinical scenario where the patient hears her own voice and breath sounds is called autophony which is seen patulous eustachian tube.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young child of a laborer presents to the OPD with abdominal distension and a fatigued facial appearance. The child’s diet mainly consists of rice water, and laboratory findings show low serum protein and albumin levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a swollen abdomen (edema), a tired face, and a diet primarily consisting of rice water (high in carbohydrates but low in protein) is indicative of Kwashiorkor. This form of severe acute malnutrition is specifically caused by a deficiency in dietary protein despite some caloric intake. The low levels of serum albumin lead to decreased oncotic pressure, resulting in the characteristic pitting edema and abdominal distension. Marasmus (Option B) is a global deficiency of all calories, presenting as severe wasting or an "old man" appearance without significant edema. Indian childhood cirrhosis (Option C) typically involves liver failure in older children. Kawasaki disease (Option D) is an acute vasculitis characterized by high fever and a "strawberry tongue". Therefore, the combination of a high-carbohydrate/low-protein diet and hypoalbuminemic edema confirms the diagnosis of Kwashiorkor
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a swollen abdomen (edema), a tired face, and a diet primarily consisting of rice water (high in carbohydrates but low in protein) is indicative of Kwashiorkor.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient with hearing loss is examined and is found to be Rinne negative at 256 Hz and 512 Hz, while Rinne positive at 1024 Hz. What is the expected air conduction and bone conduction gap?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-45 dB

The given clinical scenario of hearing loss with a negative Rinne at 256 Hz and 512 Hz and positive Rinne at 1024 Hz indicates air conduction and bone conduction gap of 30-45 dB.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, and 1024. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration, while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time.

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC).

The inferences are as follows:

• Rinne's test is considered positive (normal) when the air conduction AC>BC is seen in normal people and people with sensorineural deafness.
• It is considered negative when the BC>AC, and is seen in patients with conductive deafness. It suggests a minimum hearing loss of 15-20 dB.

A prediction of the air-bone gap can be made using tuning forks of 256, 512, and 1024 Hz:

• A Rinne test negative for 256 Hz but positive for 512 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 20-30 dB.
• A Rinne test negative for 256 and 512 Hz but positive for 1024 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 30-45 dB.
• A Rinne negative for 256, 512, and 1024 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 45-60 dB.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve? Options: 1. Abductor hallucis 2. Flexor digitorum accessorius 3. Flexor hallucis brevis 4. First lumbrical 5. First interossei

Correct answer: A. 2 and 5

The correct answer is 2 and 5.

The lateral plantar nerve supplies most intrinsic sole muscles, including flexor digitorum accessorius (quadratus plantae) and the interossei (via its deep branch).

Abductor hallucis and the first lumbrical are supplied by the medial plantar nerve, while flexor hallucis brevis has dual supply but its medial head is medial plantar—hence excluded here.

questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complaints of greenish-black material in the nasal cavity accompanied by a foul (fetid) smell. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s description of greenish-black crusts and a "merciful" foul smell (ozena) is pathognomonic for Atrophic Rhinitis. The term "merciful" refers to the fact that while the smell is offensive to others, the patient is unaware of it due to concurrent atrophy of the olfactory nerves (anosmia). This condition involves chronic atrophy of the nasal mucosa and underlying turbinate bones. Allergic rhinitis (Option A) presents with clear watery discharge, sneezing, and itching, not crusting. Rhinitis caseosa (Option C) features "cheese-like" foul material and is typically associated with extensive nasal polyps or infection. Rhinitis sicca (Option D) involves simple dryness of the mucosa, often in hot environments, but lacks the characteristic greenish crusts and ozena. Management includes regular nasal douching with alkaline solutions to clear the crusts and prevent secondary infections like Klebsiella ozaenae

questions.text: A patient with spinal cord injury shows loss of recurrent inhibition of alpha motor neurons, leading to increased muscle tone. Dysfunction of which of the following interneurons is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renshaw cell

Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord that provide recurrent inhibition to α-motor neurons.

• An α-motor neuron activates a muscle fiber and simultaneously sends a collateral branch to Renshaw cells.
• Renshaw cells release inhibitory neurotransmitters (mainly glycine).
• This inhibits the same α-motor neuron and neighboring motor neurons, preventing excessive muscle contraction.

Clinical significance:

• Loss of Renshaw cell inhibition → increased α-motor neuron activity → muscle hypertonia/spasticity.
• Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release from Renshaw cells, leading to muscle rigidity and spasms.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the cause of LH surge? FSH: Follicle-stimulating Hormone LH: Luteinizing hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estradiol

Estradiol causes LH surge. Estradiol concentrations of 200 pg/mL for 50 hours are necessary to initiate this LH surge.

Phases of the menstrual cycle :

Follicular phase (days 0–14)

* A higher FSH level at the beginning of this phase is responsible for the recruitment of the follicle cohort that contains the follicle destined for ovulation. A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.

* LH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells. During the mid-follicular phase, follicles produce greater amounts of estrogen and inhibin.

* Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus.

* FSH are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol and inhibin on the anterior pituitary.

Ovulation (day 14)

* A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of LH (LH surge). There is a small preovulatory rise in progesterone concentrations generates an FSH level surge, which occurs with the LH surge.

* Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)

* Ovulation is assumed to have occurred if the progesterone level exceeds 3 nglmL on cycle day 21. Progesterone levels are high in this phase.

* The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for the receipt of a fertilized egg.

* If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)

* The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following cells is responsible for the removal of small foreign particles trapped in the lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dust cells

Dust cells are responsible for the removal of small foreign particles trapped in the lungs.

Dust cells or pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAM) originate from the bone marrow and possess active phagocytic abilities. They play a role in engulfing small particles that manage to bypass the mucociliary escalator and reach the alveoli. They secrete substances that attract granulocytes to the lungs and substances that stimulate granulocyte and monocyte formation in the bone marrow. PAM function can also be detrimental—when they ingest large amounts of the substances in cigarette smoke or other irritants, they may release lysosomal products into the extracellular space to cause inflammation.

Other options:

Option A and C: Two major types of cells are found in the alveolar epithelium: Type I pneumocytes, the primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium), facilitate gas exchange and constitute the majority (95%) of the total surface area due to their flat surface. Additionally, the basement membrane of type I cells and the capillary endothelium are fused, minimizing the distance for gas diffusion and thereby facilitating gas exchange.

Type II cells, granular pneumocytes that produce surfactant, make up only 5% of the surface area in alveoli. These cells possess superoxide dismutase, making them more resistant to toxic oxygen radicals. As a result, they can survive, proliferate, and differentiate into Type I cells to restore the normal alveolar architecture

Option D: Clara cells, also known as Club cells, are specialized secretory cells found in the bronchioles that do not possess cilia. They act as progenitor cells and help in bronchial regeneration after injury. They also secrete essential defense markers and contribute to the composition of mucus through the secretion of a nonmucinous material containing carbohydrates and proteins.
questions.learning: Dust cells Dust cells are responsible for the removal of small foreign particles trapped in the lungs. Dust cells or pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAM) originate from the bone marrow and possess active phagocytic abilities.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 77-year-old woman is found dead in her home. On autopsy, hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture is seen. How long before her death did she probably have a myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3–7 days

Free wall rupture typically occurs during the period when the infarcted myocardium is at its structurally weakest — usually day 3 to day 7 post-MI (occasionally up to \~10 days, rarely beyond 2 weeks).

Why this timing:

• By day 1–3, coagulative necrosis has occurred, but the tissue is still reasonably cohesive.
• Around days 3–7, macrophages actively phagocytose and digest the necrotic myofibers (myomalacia cordis), and neutrophilic/granulation tissue infiltration causes maximal structural weakening — collagen deposition hasn't yet caught up to provide tensile strength.
• This makes the ventricular wall most vulnerable to rupture under intraventricular pressure during this window.
• By >2 weeks, granulation tissue matures into fibrous scar, which is mechanically stronger and resistant to rupture.

questions.text: In which condition is popcorn calcification seen ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary hamartoma

Popcorn calcification is seen in pulmonary hamartoma.

Popcorn calcification is defined as a pattern of calcification in rings and arcs that resembles popped corn kernels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient developed a lesion as shown below after 6 months of a heart surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Keloid scar

The given image shows a keloid scar.

Keloid scars are associated with elevated levels of growth factors.

A keloid scar is defined as excessive scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original incision or wound. Its etiology is unknown, but is associated with elevated levels of growth factor, deeply pigmented skin, and inherited tendency and certain areas of the body (triangle whose points are the xiphisternum and each shoulder tip).

The histology of keloid scars shows excess collagen with hypervascularity, and there is disorganized type 1 and type 3 collagen.

Keloid scars do not improve spontaneously with time and excision of the keloid scar has a high rate of recurrence.

Treatment:

* Pressure - local molds or elastic garments.

* Silicone gel sheeting.

* Intralesional triamcinolone injection

* Excision and steroid injections

* Excision and postoperative radiation (external beam or brachytherapy)

* Intralesional excision.

* Laser to reduce redness

* Vitamin E and palm oil massage

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which class of enzymes uses molecular oxygen as the hydrogen acceptor, resulting in the formation of water?
questions.explanation: In the mitochondrial electron transport chain, Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is the terminal enzyme responsible for the final reduction of oxygen. It transfers electrons to molecular oxygen, which then combines with hydrogen ions (protons) to generate water. This is the fundamental oxygen-consuming step of aerobic respiration. Catalase (Option A) breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, but does not use molecular oxygen as a hydrogen recipient. Superoxide dismutase (Option B) converts superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. Pyruvate dehydrogenase (Option D) is a mitochondrial enzyme that links glycolysis to the TCA cycle but is not part of the respiratory chain's oxygen reduction. Inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase by poisons like cyanide or carbon monoxide is lethal because it completely halts ATP production. Understanding this specific role of Complex IV is essential for grasping how the body utilizes inhaled oxygen to drive cellular energy production
questions.learning: In the mitochondrial electron transport chain, Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is the terminal enzyme responsible for the final reduction of oxygen.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the range of the firearm wound:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Close shot entry wound

A close-range firearm entry wound : Identified by the presence of burning, blackening (soot deposition) and tattooing around the entry site.

·  Central circular entry wound with inverted margins

·  Blackening due to soot, which can be wiped off

·  Tattooing due to unburnt powder particles, which cannot be wiped off

·   Possible burning or singeing of surrounding skin in very close shots

The combination of blackening and tattooing --> indicates a close-range discharge; confirms that the wound is an entry wound.

Range of Firearm Injuries (Rifle)

1. Contact Range

• Muzzle in direct contact with skin
• Cruciate (star-shaped) wound due to gas expansion under skin
• Cherry-red coloration (carboxyhemoglobin formation)
• Blackening, burning, tattooing (BBT) present inside the wound track

2. Close Range

• Muzzle near but not touching skin
• Blackening, burning, tattooing (BBT) present externally
• Grease collar (GC) and abrasion collar (AC) well developed

3. Near / Intermediate Range

• Tattooing (stippling) present (unburnt powder particles)
• No burning or blackening
• Grease collar and abrasion collar present

4. Distant Range

• Only grease collar (GC) and abrasion collar (AC) seen
• No tattooing, blackening, or burning

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The image shows changes in membrane potential during an action potential. The region marked between 4 to 5 is due to ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Efflux of K+

The region marked between 4 and 5 in the action potential curve indicates repolarization due to the efflux of K+ ions across the cell membrane.

The sequence of events during the action potential occurs in the following sequence.

1. Resting state: Both channels are closed.

2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters the cell. The membrane reaches threshold potential.

3. The sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs.

4. Sodium conductance decreases.

5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Due to K+ efflux, repolarization occurs.

6. Na+ channels are reset and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase, the K+ channels remain open and slowly return to the closed state causing after-hyperpolarization.

7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP.
questions.learning: Efflux of K+ — The region marked between 4 and 5 in the action potential curve indicates repolarization due to the efflux of K+ ions across the cell membrane.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with pain during defecation and a progressively enlarging mass at the anal verge over the past few months. Clinical evaluation and biopsy confirm squamous cell carcinoma of the anus. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: The primary treatment for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the anal canal is combined chemoradiotherapy, known as the Nigro protocol. Unlike many other GI cancers, SCC of the anus is highly sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy (typically using 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin C or cisplatin). This approach is preferred because it achieves high cure rates while preserving the anal sphincter and avoiding a permanent colostomy. Abdominoperineal resection (Option B), which involves removing the rectum and anus and creating a permanent stoma, is now reserved for patients who fail primary chemoradiation or have recurrent disease. Chemotherapy alone (Option A) is not curative for localized disease. Wide local excision (Option D) might be considered for very small, well-differentiated tumors of the anal "margin" (the skin outside), but not for carcinomas of the anal canal itself. Therefore, the sphincter-sparing combined chemoradiation remains the standard of care for anal SCC

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following can be used for the treatment of PCOD except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ulipristal

Ulipristal is not used for the treatment of polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD). It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator used as an emergency contraceptive pill.

PCOD is a complex multisystemic endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age.

Rotterdam criteria is used to diagnose PCOD. The presence of two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis.

• Oligo/amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility
• Hirsutism/acne
• Ultrasound findings:

• Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mL
• 12 or more small follicles each of 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally

Clomiphene (option A) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that is used as the first line of treatment in managing infertility. Clomiphene with dexamethasone improves the fertility rate. In resistant cases, tamoxifen or letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) (option B) can be tried.

Surgical management of PCOD includes laparoscopic ovarian drilling (option D). Indications of surgery are:

• Failed medical therapy
• Hyperstimulation occurs
• Infertile women
• Previous pregnancy losses
questions.learning: Ulipristal Ulipristal is not used for the treatment of polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD). It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator used as an emergency contraceptive pill.

questions.text: Identify the instrument given in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Morris retractor

The given image shows a Morris retractor with a single, flat transversely curved blade and a blunt projecting ridge with backward projection.

Morris retractor can be single or double-bladed. It is used to retract abdominal wall incisions, loin incisions, subcostal wounds or any wounds in depth.

It can be used to improve visibility on one side of an incision. Thus, it is valuable during the initial phase of a laparotomy.

Other options:

Option A: Deaver's retractor is a question mark-shaped stout, atraumatic retractor with a broad, gently curved long blade. It is used to retract the abdominal wall and viscera. Moist mops should be kept underneath prior to placing this retractor. It is used for major abdominal surgeries, bladder surgeries and lumbar sympathectomy.

Option C: Czerny's retractor is a superficial retractor with a thick and small blade on one side and a biflanged hook on the other side in opposite directions. It is used in hernia surgery and laparotomy, especially during closure.

Option D: Double-hook retractor consists of two hooks with a handle. It is used in excision of swellings like lipoma, neurofibroma and cyst. It is also used to hold the skin flaps when raising them.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Meissner corpuscles are present in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Papillary dermis

Meissner corpuscles are present in the papillary dermis. These corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors particularly sensitive to the movement of objects over the skin's surface and low-frequency vibrations. Their acute sensitivity plays a crucial role in tasks such as reading Braille text.

It is an elongated encapsulated nerve ending of a large myelinated sensory nerve fiber (type Aβ). Each corpuscle consists of a connective tissue capsule and a central core composed of stacked modified Schwann cells. Meissner's corpuscles are found in nonhairy areas of the skin, especially in fingertips, lips, and other regions where spatial touch perception is highly developed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 70-year-old man who had gastrointestinal surgery one month ago presents with a palpable bulge at the surgical site. On examination, a reducible incisional hernia measuring 12 cm is noted. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
options: Prescribe an abdominal belt for daily use
Advice observation and reassessment in six months
questions.explanation: The patient has a large (12 cm), symptomatic incisional hernia. Because the hernia is reducible and the patient is relatively recent from their primary surgery (1 month), the most appropriate next step for definitive management is surgical repair. Modern standards dictate that for an incisional hernia of this size, a mesh repair (either laparoscopic or open) is mandatory to reduce the very high rate of recurrence associated with primary suture closure. Laparoscopic closure without mesh (Option D) is incorrect due to the high failure rate. While an abdominal belt (Option B) can provide temporary symptomatic relief, it is not a "management step" toward a cure. Observation (Option C) is generally only for asymptomatic patients who are poor surgical candidates. Laparoscopic Intraperitoneal Onlay Mesh (IPOM) is a common technique for such repairs, offering less postoperative pain and faster recovery. Preoperative optimization, including weight loss and smoking cessation, is critical for surgical success
questions.learning: The patient has a large (12 cm), symptomatic incisional hernia. Because the hernia is reducible and the patient is relatively recent from their primary surgery (1 month), the most appropriate next step for definitive management is surgical repair.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with itching in the axilla. On microscopic examination of the skin scrapings, a red pigment-producing fungus with pencil-shaped macroconidia is seen. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trichophyton rubrum

The most likely organism based on the given history and image is Trichophyton rubrum. The colonies appear velvety and a deep red, non-diffusible pigment is seen when viewed from the reverse side of the colony. A few long and pencil-shaped macroconidia can be seen.

Trichophyton is a dermatophytic fungi that can infect hair, skin, or nails. Dermatophytes infect only the keratinized tissue and have keratinases that can digest keratin. There are 3 genera of dermatophytes:

• Trichophyton - The colonies may appear powdery, waxy, or velvety with pigmentation characteristics of different species.
• Epidermophyton - It infects the skin and nails, but not the hair. The colonies appear powdery and greenish-yellow.
• Microsporum - It infects the hair and skin, but not the nails. The colonies may appear cotton-like, velvety, or powdery, with white to brown pigmentation.

T. rubrum causes tinea corporis.  It results from the invasion and proliferation of the causal fungi in the stratum corneum, with lesions on the trunk and limbs. The lesions are usually well-defined and circular with a raised edge. It can also cause tinea pedis, tinea cruris, and onychomycosis.

Other options:

Option A: The colonies of T. violaceus are very slow-growing, waxy with a violet/purple pigment. They have distorted hyphae, with conidia seen rarely.

Option C: T. tonsurans has a cream or yellowish colony with central furrows. Microconidia are abundantly seen. Thick-walled, irregular macroconidia are also seen.

Option D: Colonies of T. schoenleinii are smooth, waxy and brownish. Hyphal swellings are seen along with chlamydospores and favic chandelier.
questions.learning: Trichophyton rubrum — The most likely organism based on the given history and image is Trichophyton rubrum. The colonies appear velvety and a deep red, non-diffusible pigment is seen when viewed from the reverse side of the colony.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female undergoes a methylene blue 3 swab test and the middle swab is stained with blue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vesicovaginal fistula

The given clinical scenario with methylene blue swab test showing staining of middle swab is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula.

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of genital fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the genital tract and the urinary tract. It can be classified as simple or complicated. Their features are given in the table below.

Simple VVF
Complicated VVF

Size ≤ 3 cm
Size > 3 cm

Located near the cuff or supra-trigonal
Located away from the cuff / there is the involvement of trigone

No prior malignancy
Pelvic malignancy present

No prior radiation
Prior radiation therapy

The vaginal length remains normal
Vaginal length shortened

Vesicovaginal fistulae occur mostly due to obstetric injuries such as prolonged labor, and instrumental or manipulative deliveries. Patients present with true incontinence characterized by constant dribbling of urine. The presence of urine in the undergarments is uncomfortable and leads to pruritus and excoriation of the genital area.

Investigations to be performed include

* Urine culture and treatment of infection if required

* Ultrasound of the kidney, ureter, and bladder

* Intravenous pyelography

* Methylene blue - 3 swab test if the fistula is small. Here, methylene blue is injected into the bladder via the catheter, and three sterile swabs are placed into the vaginal cavity.

* The uppermost swab gets wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter, seen in the ureterovaginal fistula

* The middle swab gets stained - the leak is from the bladder, seen in vesicovaginal fistula

* The lowermost swab gets stained- the leak is from the urethra, seen in the urethrovaginal fistula

* Cystourethroscopy helps in fistula localization, determination of its proximity to the ureteral orifices, inspection for multiple fistula sites, etc.

Vesicovaginal fistula is treated surgically. It can be attempted after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside and clear the infection. After this, the Latzko procedure can be performed. Here, the vaginal epithelium around the fistula is removed and the edges are approximated. The Chassar Moir technique can also be attempted. Here, the vagina and bladder are separated and sutured into two layers taking care to avoid tension and overlapping suture lines.
questions.learning: Vesicovaginal fistula — The given clinical scenario with methylene blue swab test showing staining of middle swab is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with glaucoma. What is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prostaglandin analogues

Prostaglandin analogues are the drug of choice for glaucoma.  This class of anti-glaucoma drugs acts by increasing the uveo-scleral outflow.

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog and a commonly used medication for glaucoma. Prostaglandin analogs are often preferred due to their effectiveness and once-daily dosing convenience.

Topical PGF2 alpha (prostaglandin) analogs are used as a first line in glaucoma. Latanoprost is the most commonly used anti-glaucoma medication. Other prostaglandin analogues are travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluprost, and unoprostone.

Mechanism of action: It reduces intraocular pressure by altering the ciliary muscle tension and improving the outflow of the aqueous humor.

Adverse effects:

* Blurring of vision

* Iris pigmentation

* Thickening and darkening of eyelashes

* Macular edema especially in aphakic patients.

* Orbital fat atrophy

Pearl PF1386: Antiglaucoma drugs: Mechanism of lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) at a glance

Drugs that increase trabecular outflow

* Miotics (e.g., pilocarpine)

* Epinephrine, dipivefrine

* Bimatoprost

Drugs that increase uveoscleral outflow

* Prostaglandins (latanoprost)

* Epinephrine, dipivefrine

* Brimonidine

* Apraclonidine

Drugs that decrease aqueous production

* Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide, dorzolamide)

* Alpha receptor stimulators in ciliary process (e.g., epinephrine, dipivefrine, clonidine, brimonidine, apraclonidine)

* Beta-blockers

Hyperosmotic agents - (e.g., glycerol, mannitol, urea)
questions.learning: Prostaglandin analogues Prostaglandin analogues are the drug of choice for glaucoma. This class of anti-glaucoma drugs acts by increasing the uveo-scleral outflow.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the medical term for a person who has a fear of tall buildings and looking down from heights?
questions.explanation: The specific, intense fear of heights, including looking down from tall buildings, is called Acrophobia. Agoraphobia (Option A) is the fear of being in situations or places (like open spaces or crowds) where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during a panic attack. Claustrophobia (Option C) is the fear of enclosed or small spaces. Nomophobia (Option D) is the fear of being without a mobile phone or being out of cellular contact. Acrophobia is one of the most common specific phobias and can cause significant distress or avoidance behavior. Patients may experience dizziness, sweating, or a sense of "pulling" toward the edge when exposed to heights. Treatment usually involves Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), specifically exposure therapy, where the person is gradually and systematically exposed to feared heights in a safe environment to reduce the anxiety response

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old female presents with generalized swelling, facial puffiness, hypertension, and frothy urine. She also reports a history of recurrent oral ulcers, photosensitivity, and intermittent joint pain. Investigations reveal positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, decreased serum C3 and C4 levels, and proteinuria of 4.2 g/day. What is the most likely underlying mechanism responsible for her renal injury?
options: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis causing glomerular damage
Formation and deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli with subsequent complement activation
Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation and deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli with subsequent complement activation

The patient has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with lupus nephritis, characterized by proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), edema, hypertension, positive ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, and low C3/C4 levels, photosensitivity, oral ulcers and arthritis. The renal injury in lupus nephritis is caused by Type III hypersensitivity, in which circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli, activate the classical complement pathway, and trigger inflammation, leading to glomerular damage.

Why not the other options?

• A. ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis causing glomerular damage: Seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; typically ANCA-positive and complement levels are normal.
• B. T-lymphocyte-mediated cytotoxic injury (Type IV hypersensitivity): Characteristic of diseases such as contact dermatitis and type 1 diabetes mellitus, not lupus nephritis.
• D. Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane: Seen in Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease), which presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a patient with a corneal scar whose visual acuity improves when tested with a pinhole, what is the most likely cause of the reduced vision?
questions.explanation: When a patient's visual acuity improves during the pinhole test, it definitively indicates that the vision loss is due to a refractive error rather than primary organic pathology. The pinhole works by blocking peripheral distorted light rays and allowing only central parallel rays to reach the macula. In a patient with a corneal scar, the surface of the cornea becomes uneven, leading specifically to irregular astigmatism (Option C). This type of astigmatism cannot be corrected by standard glasses but is partially bypassed by the pinhole. Vision loss from Glaucoma (Option A), which involves optic nerve damage, would not improve with a pinhole. Malingering (Option B) is a psychological state where the patient purposefully feigns loss. A Cataract (Option D) involves a clouded lens; while some cataracts allow minor improvement with a pinhole, the direct link between a corneal scar and distorted light makes irregular astigmatism the most accurate clinical cause. Rigid gas permeable contact lenses are the preferred correction for this condition
questions.learning: When a patient's visual acuity improves during the pinhole test, it definitively indicates that the vision loss is due to a refractive error rather than primary organic pathology.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with penetrating chest trauma and tracheal deviation. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. E-FAST

E-FAST (Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is a rapid bedside ultrasound used in trauma to detect:

• Pneumothorax
• Hemothorax
• Pericardial tamponade
• Intra-abdominal bleeding

It is fast, non-invasive, and performed immediately in the ER.

In a trauma patient, the goal is to quickly identify life-threatening causes without delaying care.

E-FAST allows immediate detection of:

• Collapsed lung
• Pleural fluid
• Blood in thorax or abdomen

This guides urgent interventions like chest tube insertion.

❌ A) Needle decompression in 2nd intercostal space

This is done only if tension pneumothorax is clearly suspected and the patient is unstable.

Here, the diagnosis should first be confirmed quickly with E-FAST.

❌ B) CT scan

CT provides detailed imaging, but:

• Too slow
• Requires patient transfer

Not suitable as the immediate step in trauma resuscitation.

❌ D) Oxygen at 100%

Oxygen is supportive but does not diagnose the cause of tracheal deviation.

In chest trauma with suspected pneumothorax or hemothorax:

Immediate bedside evaluation → E-FAST

Then proceed to:

• Chest tube
• Needle decompression
• Further imaging if stable

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Match the following question on signs of testicular torsion:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-A, 2-B, 3-E, 4-D, 5-C

Testicular torsion is a urological emergency caused by twisting of the spermatic cord → acute ischemia, and is primarily a clinical diagnosis.

| Sign | Finding | Mechanism

| ---- | ------- | ---------

| Prehn sign | Pain not relieved by elevation of the testis (negative Prehn sign) | Distinguishes torsion from epididymitis

| Gouverneur sign | Horizontal (transverse) lie of the affected testis | Twisting of the spermatic cord rotates the testis

| Angell sign | Horizontal lie of the contralateral testis due to bilateral bell-clapper deformity | Indicates bilateral predisposition; supports bilateral orchidopexy

| Brunzel sign | High-riding (elevated) testis | Shortening of the twisted spermatic cord pulls the testis upward

| Ger sign | Absent cremasteric reflex | Ischemia and twisting abolish the reflex

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Pacemaker generating the rhythm for breathing is ________
options: Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pre-Bőtzinger complex

Pre-Botzinger complex generates the rhythm for automated breathing.

• These are also known as pacemaker cells located in the medulla.
• These are the first set of neurons that initiate inspiration.
• These neurons discharge rhythmically, and they produce rhythmic discharges in the phrenic motor neurons.

Breathing is under the control of both the following:

• Voluntary control: Located in the cerebral cortex (via corticospinal tract)
• Automatic control: Driven by pacemaker cells in the medulla (Pre-Botzinger complex). These activate motor neurons via cervical (Phrenic nerve innervating diaphragm) and thoracic spinal cord (external intercostal muscle).

There is a reciprocal innervation to expiratory and inspiratory muscles in that motor neurons supplying expiratory muscles are inactive when motor neurons supplying inspiratory muscles are active, and vice versa.

Inspiration

Initiation
Pre-Botzinger complex (Pacemaker cells) in Medulla

Maintenance
Apneustic center in lower Pons stimulates Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla

Termination
Apneustic center inhibited by Vagus and Pneumotaxic center

Regulation of expiration: During quiet breathing, expiration is a passive process; there is no firing of neurons. Ventral respiratory group of neurons are involved in forceful expiration like during exercise.

Mnemonic DIVE: Dorsal respiratory group for Inspiration and Ventral respiratory group for Expiration.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is undergoing pubertal changes. Her tanner stage is stage 4 for breast development and pubic hair scale. Which of the following pubertal changes is not due to estrogen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pubic and axillary hair growth

Pubarche or development of axillary and pubic hair is not due to estrogen. It is due to testosterone (in both the sexes).

Puberty in females :

* Involves the beginning of menstrual cycles (menarche), breast development (thelarche), and an increase in adrenal androgen secretion (adrenarche).

* Estradiol induces the development of secondary sex characteristics, including the breasts and reproductive tract, and increased fat in the hips.

* Estrogens also regulate the growth spurt at puberty, vaginal cornification and cervical mucus production, induce closure of the epiphyses, have a positive effect in maintaining bone formation, and can antagonize the degrading actions of parathyroid hormone on bone.

In young girls before puberty the vaginal epithelium is thin and comprised of only basal and parabasal layers. During the reproductive years, the vaginal epithelium thickens and develops a distinct cornified layer due to the influence of estrogen. Cervical mucous production and menstruation are also changes occuring under the influence of estrogen and also progesterone.
questions.learning: Pubic and axillary hair growth Pubarche or development of axillary and pubic hair is not due to estrogen. It is due to testosterone (in both the sexes).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male who is a professional trumpet blower presented with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, there is a gurgling sound when compressing the swelling. As the X-ray neck was inconclusive a CT neck was taken which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laryngocele

The given CT image along with the examination finding of Bryce sign is suggestive of laryngocoele.

Laryngocoele:

* Air-filled cavity within the larynx developing in the saccule.

* The patient presents with a neck swelling that is soft and compressible.

* Bryce sign: on compressing the swelling, there is a gurgling sound.

It is seen in trumpet players, glass-blowers, or weight lifters due to raised transglottic air pressure. It presents with hoarseness, cough, and if large, causes obstruction of the airway.

Types of laryngocoele are:

* Internal - confined within the larynx and presents as distension of false cord and aryepiglottic fold.

* External - the distended saccule herniates through the thyroid membrane and presents in the neck. It presents as a reducible swelling in the neck, increasing in size on coughing or performing Valsalva manoeuvres.

* Mixed - both external and internal compounds are seen

Diagnosis is done by indirect laryngoscopy, soft tissue AP and lateral views of the neck x-ray with Valsalva. CT scan helps to find out the extent of the lesion. External type is managed by surgical excision through an external neck incision. Internal type is managed by marsupialization and endoscopic carbon dioxide laser resection.

Other options:

Option A: Zenker diverticulum or pharyngeal pouch is a pulsion-pseudodiverticulum and results from herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle (or dehiscence of Killian). Killian’s triangle represents a weak space located between two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle.

Option C: A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal fistula communication between the Esophagus and Trachea. Type C lesion is associated with proximal esophageal atresia and distal TEF, the proximal blind pouch ends approximately at the distance of one or two vertebral bodies from the distal TEF.

Option D: A tonsillar cyst is due to blockage of a tonsillar crypt and appears as a yellowish swelling over the tonsil. Very often it is symptomless. It can be easily drained.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with known history of leprosy presents to the clinic. On examination, a thickened nerve is noted in the neck (as shown in the image). Which of the following nerves is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Great auricular nerve

In leprosy, superficial sensory nerves are commonly involved, leading to palpable thickening.

The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) runs superficially over the sternocleidomastoid in the neck and supplies the skin over the parotid region and lower auricle, making it a classic nerve affected in leprosy.

Auriculotemporal and lesser occipital nerves are less commonly thickened, while the spinal accessory nerve is motor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which strain of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is most commonly linked to the development of cervical cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 16, 18

Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types leads to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and eventually cervical carcinoma.

The two most important oncogenic strains are:

• HPV 16
• HPV 18

Together they cause \~70% of cervical cancers worldwide.

High-risk HPV strains produce two key oncogenic proteins:

| Viral Protein | Target | Effect

| ------------- | ------ | ------

| E6 | p53 tumor suppressor | Inhibits apoptosis

| E7 | Rb tumor suppressor | Uncontrolled cell cycle

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A dead body shows the following finding as in the image. What is the case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Smothering

Smothering is a form of asphyxial death caused by external obstruction of the mouth and nose, typically by a hand, cloth, or soft object.

• Abrasions and bruises around mouth and nose
• Lacerations of lips and gums
• Teeth impressions on lips (bite marks)
• Blood-stained mouth due to struggle
• Possible nail marks on face

Mechanism:

• Obstruction of external air passages → hypoxia → death
• Often associated with struggle, especially in homicidal cases

Why not other options:

• Hanging: Ligature mark on neck
• Gagging: Obstruction inside mouth, not external compression
• Garroting: Ligature strangulation with force from behind
